101243.q: What happens to the molecules in a mass spectrometer before they are sorted by mass?
101243.e: Only charged particles can be deflected by electric and magnetic fields. That is why the molecules are ionised first.
101243.m: In a mass spectrometer, molecules are first turned into ions.

101244.q: A mass spectrum shows two molecular ion peaks 2 units apart with an intensity ratio of about 3 to 1. Which element does the compound probably contain?
101244.e: Chlorine consists of about 76 per cent ³⁵Cl and about 24 per cent ³⁷Cl. This gives the typical ratio of about 3 to 1 between M and M+2.
101244.m: An M+2 peak a third the height of the molecular ion peak points to a chlorine atom.

101245.q: Which isotope pattern does the molecular ion of a compound with exactly one bromine atom show?
a: M and M+2 about equally high
M+2 about a third of M
M+1 about half as high as M
Only a single peak at M
101245.e: Bromine occurs as ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br in almost equal proportions. That is why M and M+2 appear almost equally strong.
101245.m: With bromine, the M and M+2 peaks are almost equally high.

101246.q: Why do molecules often break into several fragments during electron impact ionisation?
a: The colliding electrons transfer a lot of energy
The magnetic field tears them apart
They react with oxygen from the air
101246.e: Fast electrons knock an electron out of the molecule and also give off energy. The ion therefore often breaks into typical fragments that act like a fingerprint.
101246.m: High-energy electrons break molecules into typical fragments.

101247.q: Why do proteins need particularly gentle ionisation in a mass spectrometer?
a: Otherwise the large molecules break into many fragments
101247.e: Large biomolecules are delicate and break apart with harsh methods. Gentle techniques such as electrospray ionisation bring them into the instrument intact.
101247.m: Large biomolecules must be ionised gently so that they stay whole.

101248.q: In a time-of-flight mass spectrometer (TOF), which ions with the same charge reach the detector first?
a: The ions with the greatest polarity
All ions at the same time
101248.e: All ions get the same kinetic energy, so light ions fly faster. The flight time can therefore be used to calculate m/z.
101248.m: In a time-of-flight analyser, light ions arrive before heavy ones.

101249.q: What did the first mass spectrographs around 1920 show about many chemical elements?
a: Their atoms all weigh the same
101249.e: With the mass spectrograph, atoms of different masses were found in many non-radioactive elements. This also explained atomic masses that are not whole numbers.
101249.m: Mass spectrometry revealed the isotopes of many elements.

101250.q: At which m/z value would you expect the molecular ion peak of ethanol C₂H₆O (C 12, H 1, O 16)?
101250.e: 2 · 12 + 6 · 1 + 16 = 46. For the singly charged molecular ion, m/z equals the molecular mass.
101250.m: The molecular ion peak shows the mass of the whole molecule.

101251.q: Which property of certain atomic nuclei does NMR spectroscopy use?
101251.e: Nuclei with nuclear spin, such as the hydrogen nucleus, have a magnetic moment. In a strong magnetic field they absorb radio waves of a particular frequency.
101251.m: NMR uses the magnetism of atomic nuclei.

101252.q: What does the abbreviation NMR stand for?
101252.e: NMR stands for “nuclear magnetic resonance”. It is also called nuclear spin resonance.

101253.q: How many groups of different hydrogen atoms does ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) show in the ¹H NMR spectrum?
101253.e: The H atoms of the CH₃ group, the CH₂ group and the OH group each have a different chemical environment. Each group gives its own signal.
101253.m: Hydrogen atoms in the same environment give the same NMR signal.

101254.q: What does the integral of a signal in the ¹H NMR spectrum tell you?
101254.e: The area under a signal is proportional to the number of hydrogen nuclei producing it. This lets you work out the ratio of the different groups of protons.
101254.m: The signal area in the proton spectrum shows how many hydrogen atoms are involved.

101255.q: What does it mean when two hydrogen atoms appear in different places in the NMR spectrum?
a: They have a different chemical environment
101255.e: Neighbouring atoms and bonds shield each nucleus from the magnetic field to a different degree. That is why the signals appear at different chemical shifts.
101255.m: The position of an NMR signal reveals the atom's environment.

101256.q: Which Zurich-born physicist shared the 1952 Nobel Prize in Physics with Edward Purcell for developing nuclear magnetic resonance?
101256.e: Felix Bloch was born in Zurich in 1905 and studied at ETH. He and Purcell independently developed methods for measuring nuclear magnetic resonance in solids and liquids.
101256.m: Felix Bloch from Zurich is one of the founders of nuclear magnetic resonance.

101257.q: Why are samples for ¹H NMR usually dissolved in deuterated solvents such as CDCl₃?
a: So that the solvent does not produce a large proton signal
So that the sample evaporates faster
So that the sample does not oxidise
So that the molecular mass increases
101257.e: Deuterium has a completely different resonance frequency from ¹H and does not appear in the proton spectrum. The instrument also uses the deuterium signal to stabilise the magnetic field.
101257.m: Deuterated solvents stop the solvent from covering up the proton spectrum.

101258.q: Which medical imaging method is based on the same physical principle as NMR spectroscopy?
101258.e: Magnetic resonance imaging measures the nuclear magnetic resonance of hydrogen nuclei in the body. Field gradients link the signal to a location.
101258.m: Magnetic resonance imaging is nuclear magnetic resonance applied to people.

101259.q: What advantage does an NMR spectrometer with a stronger magnetic field bring, for example 800 MHz instead of 300 MHz?
a: A shorter half-life of the sample
Measurement without nuclei that have spin
101259.e: With a stronger field, the frequency gaps between signals and the population difference of the spin states increase. Signals overlap less and are stronger.
101259.m: A stronger magnetic field makes NMR spectra sharper and more sensitive.

101260.q: What did Richard R. Ernst receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for in 1991?
a: For contributions to high-resolution NMR spectroscopy
101260.e: Ernst developed Fourier transform NMR and multidimensional NMR spectroscopy. He received the prize alone.
101260.m: Richard Ernst was honoured in 1991 for modern NMR spectroscopy.

101261.q: In which Swiss city was Richard R. Ernst born in 1933?
101261.e: Ernst came from Winterthur and also died there in 2021. He studied and did research at ETH Zurich.
101261.m: The Nobel Prize winner Richard Ernst was born in Winterthur.

101262.q: At which university was Richard R. Ernst a professor for most of his career?
101262.e: Ernst did his doctorate at ETH Zurich and returned there as a researcher in 1968. He later became professor of physical chemistry there.
101262.m: Richard Ernst taught and did research at ETH Zurich.

101263.q: Which mathematical method did Ernst use to obtain a whole NMR spectrum from a short radio frequency pulse?
101263.e: Ernst excited all the nuclei at once with a pulse and broke the fading signal down into its frequencies with the Fourier transform. This made measurements much faster and more sensitive.
101263.m: The Fourier transform turns the NMR time signal into a spectrum.

101264.q: Which medical imaging method, like Richard Ernst's NMR spectroscopy, is based on nuclear magnetic resonance?
101264.e: MRI uses the same principle as NMR: atomic nuclei in a magnetic field send out radio signals. Ernst's methods also contributed to the development of MRI.
101264.m: MRI and NMR are based on nuclear magnetic resonance.

101265.q: What do chemists mainly use NMR spectroscopy for?
a: To work out the structure of molecules
101265.e: NMR shows how the atoms in a molecule are connected. It is one of the most important methods for working out structures.
101265.m: NMR tells you how a molecule is built.

101266.q: Which works of art did Richard R. Ernst collect and study with spectroscopic methods?
101266.e: Ernst was a great collector of Tibetan thangka paintings. He used Raman spectroscopy to analyse the pigments used.
101266.m: Richard Ernst studied the colours of Tibetan scroll paintings with spectroscopy.

101267.q: What does an NMR instrument need to align the atomic nuclei of a sample?
101267.e: Atomic nuclei with nuclear spin behave like tiny magnets and line up in a magnetic field. A radio pulse disturbs this alignment, and the nuclei send out measurable signals.
101267.m: NMR instruments work with strong magnetic fields.

101268.q: What did Kurt Wüthrich receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for in 2002?
a: For determining the structure of biomolecules in solution by NMR
101268.e: Wüthrich showed how to use NMR to determine the three-dimensional structure of proteins in solution. The other half of the prize went to Fenn and Tanaka for mass spectrometry.
101268.m: Kurt Wüthrich was the first to determine protein structures in solution with NMR.

101269.q: Which canton does the chemistry Nobel Prize winner Kurt Wüthrich come from?
101269.e: Wüthrich was born in 1938 in Aarberg in the Bernese Seeland and studied at the University of Bern. He later did research at ETH Zurich.
101269.m: Kurt Wüthrich comes from the canton of Bern.

101270.q: What advantage does determining protein structures by NMR have over X-ray crystallography?
a: The protein does not have to be crystallised
It only works with large proteins
It always gives the molecular mass
101270.e: Many proteins are hard to crystallise. With NMR they are measured in solution, closer to their natural environment.
101270.m: With NMR you study proteins in solution, without any crystal.

101271.q: Which particles in the protein mainly provide the measured signals in Wüthrich's NMR method?
101271.e: In nuclear magnetic resonance, atomic nuclei in a strong magnetic field respond to radio waves. Proteins contain a great many hydrogen atoms, whose nuclei are easy to measure.
101271.m: Protein NMR mainly measures the signals of hydrogen nuclei.

101272.q: At which university did Kurt Wüthrich teach as professor of biophysics?
101272.e: Wüthrich did research at ETH Zurich from the late 1960s and became professor of biophysics there. He also did research at the Scripps Research Institute in California.
101272.m: Kurt Wüthrich did research as a biophysicist at ETH Zurich.

101273.q: Besides Switzerland, in which country did Kurt Wüthrich also do research as a professor?
101273.e: From 2001, Wüthrich also held a professorship at the Scripps Research Institute in California. He travelled back and forth between Zurich and the USA.
101273.m: Kurt Wüthrich did research in Zurich and in California.

101274.q: In 1996, Wüthrich's group used NMR to determine the structure of which protein linked to the disease BSE?
101274.e: Prions are misfolded proteins that cause diseases such as BSE. Wüthrich's group determined the structure of the normal prion protein of the mouse.
101274.m: In 1996, Wüthrich's group worked out the structure of the prion protein with NMR.

101275.q: Why is it so important to know the three-dimensional structure of a protein?
a: The shape determines how the protein works
The shape determines the blood group
The shape determines the age of the cell
The shape determines the colour of the protein
101275.e: Enzymes, receptors and antibodies only work if their shape fits exactly. Knowing the structure helps, for example, to develop medicines in a more targeted way.

101276.q: For which method did Jacques Dubochet from Vaud receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2017?
101276.e: Dubochet shared the prize with Joachim Frank and Richard Henderson. Cryo-electron microscopy makes it possible to image frozen biomolecules in their natural shape.
101276.m: Jacques Dubochet received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for cryo-electron microscopy.

101277.q: Which canton does the chemistry Nobel Prize winner Jacques Dubochet come from?
101277.e: Dubochet was born in 1942 in Aigle in the canton of Vaud. He later became a professor at the University of Lausanne.
101277.m: Jacques Dubochet is from Vaud and did his research in Lausanne.

101278.q: At which university was Jacques Dubochet a professor from 1987?
101278.e: After his time in Heidelberg, Dubochet moved to the University of Lausanne. There he headed the Laboratory for Ultrastructural Analysis.
101278.m: Jacques Dubochet taught at the University of Lausanne.

101279.q: What was Dubochet's crucial contribution to cryo-electron microscopy?
a: Freezing water so fast that it sets like glass
101279.e: When frozen in a flash, water does not form a crystal lattice but amorphous, glassy ice. In this way, biomolecules keep their natural shape.
101279.m: Dubochet vitrified water so that biomolecules stay undamaged when frozen.

101280.q: Why are normal ice crystals a problem in samples for electron microscopy?
a: They scatter the electron beam and destroy structures
101280.e: Ice crystals strongly diffract the electrons and cover up the image of the molecules. As they grow, they can also deform delicate structures.
101280.m: Ice crystals spoil the electron microscope image and damage biomolecules.

101281.q: Which coolant is used to keep samples very cold during measurement in cryo-electron microscopy?
101281.e: Liquid nitrogen boils at about minus 196 °C. This keeps the glassy ice of the sample stable so that it does not crystallise.
101281.m: In cryo-electron microscopy, samples are cooled with liquid nitrogen.

101282.q: What does the term “vitrification”, which Dubochet used for his freezing method, mean?
101282.e: The Latin word “vitrum” means glass. In vitrification, water sets so quickly that it becomes solid and glassy without crystals.
101282.m: Vitrification means turning into glass: water sets without ice crystals.

101283.q: Why do biological samples dry out in an ordinary electron microscope?
a: Because there is a vacuum in the microscope
Because the electron beam breaks water down chemically
Because the microscope is strongly heated
Because the sample is stained first
101283.e: Electrons need a high vacuum, otherwise they collide with air molecules. In a vacuum, liquid water evaporates immediately, whereas frozen water is kept.
101283.m: In the vacuum of an electron microscope, liquid water would evaporate immediately.

101284.q: Which gas is often used as the carrier gas in gas chromatography?
101284.e: The carrier gas must be unreactive and carry the sample through the column. Helium, hydrogen or nitrogen are common.
101284.m: An inert carrier gas such as helium forms the mobile phase in gas chromatography.

101285.q: Which property must substances have so that they can be analysed directly by gas chromatography?
a: They can be vaporised without breaking down
101285.e: The sample is vaporised in the injector and must travel through the column as a gas. Substances that break down in the process are unsuitable or must be converted first.
101285.m: For gas chromatography, substances must vaporise without breaking down.

101286.q: In gas chromatography, which measured value is used to identify a substance under fixed conditions?
101286.e: The retention time is the time from injection until the signal appears at the detector. Under the same conditions it is characteristic of a substance.
101286.m: The retention time is a substance's fingerprint in gas chromatography.

101287.q: What does a gas chromatograph produce at the end of a measurement?
a: a chromatogram with one signal for each separated substance
an X-ray image of the sample
101287.e: The detector at the end of the column registers each substance that arrives there. This produces a diagram in which each substance appears as its own peak.
101287.m: In the chromatogram, each separated substance appears as its own peak.

101288.q: Why is the oven temperature raised during many gas chromatography measurements?
a: So that substances that are hard to vaporise also leave the column quickly
So that the carrier gas becomes heavier
So that the detector cools down
So that the column gets longer
101288.e: At a low temperature, easily vaporised substances are separated well. Heating then lets the less volatile substances leave the column in a reasonable time.
101288.m: A temperature programme separates volatile and less volatile substances in one run.

101289.q: On what principle does chromatography separate a mixture?
a: The substances are distributed differently between the mobile and stationary phases.
The substances are sorted by their radioactivity.
The substances are deflected in a magnetic field.
The substances are filtered by their colour.
101289.e: A substance that sticks strongly to the stationary phase moves slowly. A substance that prefers to stay in the mobile phase moves quickly. This separates the substances.
101289.m: Chromatography separates substances by how they are distributed between two phases.

101290.q: Other things being equal, which substance usually leaves the column of a gas chromatograph first?
a: the substance with the lowest boiling point
the substance with the highest boiling point
the substance with the greatest molecular mass
the substance with the strongest colour
101290.e: Volatile substances stay almost entirely in the carrier gas and are carried quickly through the column. Less volatile substances spend longer in the stationary phase.
101290.m: Volatile substances appear first in gas chromatography.

101291.q: What is the long, thin tube called in which the substances are separated in gas chromatography?
101291.e: The column is often many metres long and coiled up. It sits in an oven, and the carrier gas carries the sample through it.
101291.m: The separation takes place in a long, thin column.

101292.q: Which combination of two methods separates mixtures and at the same time identifies the components from their fragments?
101292.e: Gas chromatography separates the mixture and the attached mass spectrometer gives a spectrum for each substance. GC-MS is standard in environmental, doping and food analysis.
101292.m: Combining gas chromatography and mass spectrometry separates and identifies at the same time.

101293.q: What is the aim of green chemistry?
a: designing chemical processes with as little waste and danger as possible
carrying out all reactions at room temperature
101293.e: Green chemistry aims to avoid waste, toxic substances and energy use right from the planning of a synthesis. Paul Anastas and John Warner summed this up in twelve principles in 1998.
101293.m: Green chemistry avoids waste and danger right from the planning stage.

101294.q: Which type of reaction basically has an atom economy of 100 per cent?
101294.e: In an addition, all the atoms of the reactants are built into a single product. No by-products form.
101294.m: Addition reactions build all the atoms of the starting materials into the product.

101295.q: What is the atom economy of the reaction CH₃Br + NaOH to CH₃OH + NaBr, using M(CH₃Br) = 94.9 g/mol, M(NaOH) = 40.0 g/mol and M(CH₃OH) = 32.0 g/mol?
101295.e: Atom economy is the molar mass of the desired product divided by the sum of the reactant molar masses. 32.0 / (94.9 + 40.0) = 32.0 / 134.9 gives about 0.24.
101295.m: Atom economy compares the mass of the target product with the mass of all the starting materials.

101296.q: The E-factor is the mass of waste divided by the mass of product. A synthesis produces 2 kg of product and 50 kg of waste. What is the E-factor?
101296.e: 50 kg of waste divided by 2 kg of product gives 25. So 25 kg of waste is produced for every kilogram of product.
101296.m: The smaller the E-factor, the less waste per kilogram of product.

101298.q: Which supercritical fluid is used as an environmentally friendly solvent, for example to decaffeinate coffee?
101298.e: Supercritical CO₂ is non-toxic, non-flammable and easy to remove as a gas after extraction. In this way it replaces organic solvents.
101298.m: Supercritical carbon dioxide is a green solvent with no toxic residues.

101299.q: Why does green chemistry prefer catalysts to stoichiometric reagents?
a: Catalysts are not used up and save waste
Catalysts always raise the yield to 100 per cent
101299.e: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up itself. Stoichiometric reagents, by contrast, usually end up as waste.
101299.m: Catalysts save raw materials because they are not used up in the reaction.

101300.q: Why are syntheses with fewer reaction steps considered more environmentally friendly?
a: They need less energy and solvent and produce less waste.
They always give more colourful products.
They need no starting materials at all.
101300.e: Every step needs solvents, energy and purification, and some product is lost. Fewer steps therefore save raw materials and avoid waste.
101300.m: Fewer synthesis steps mean less waste.

101301.q: Why are PFAS often called “forever chemicals”?
a: Because the carbon-fluorine bond is extremely stable
Because they break down immediately in water
Because they only occur in space
101301.e: The C-F bond is one of the strongest single bonds in organic chemistry. That is why PFAS are practically not broken down in the environment.
101301.m: Because of the strong carbon-fluorine bond, PFAS stay in the environment almost for ever.

101302.q: What does “perfluorinated” mean for an alkyl chain?
a: All the hydrogen atoms on the carbon are replaced by fluorine
The chain contains exactly one fluorine atom
The chain is closed into a ring
The chain contains fluorine and chlorine
101302.e: The prefix “per” means completely. In a perfluorinated chain, every carbon atom carries only fluorine instead of hydrogen.
101302.m: In a perfluorinated chain, every hydrogen on the carbon is replaced by fluorine.

101303.q: Which two properties make PFAS so popular for coating textiles and paper?
a: They conduct electricity and are magnetic
101303.e: PFAS chains are both hydrophobic and lipophobic. That is why they were used for outdoor jackets, pizza boxes and non-stick coatings.
101303.m: PFAS repel water and grease at the same time.

101304.q: Which fluoroplastic, known for non-stick pans, was discovered by chance by Roy Plunkett in 1938?
101304.e: In a gas cylinder of tetrafluoroethylene, Plunkett found a white powder that turned out to be a polymer. PTFE is very unreactive and heat-resistant.
101304.m: Polytetrafluoroethylene was discovered by chance in 1938 and coats non-stick pans.

101305.q: In which firefighting agent were PFAS used in large quantities for a long time, which now pollutes soil and groundwater in many places?
101305.e: Fluorine-containing foams form a film that is particularly good at putting out burning liquids such as kerosene. This is how a lot of PFAS got into the soil at airfields and training grounds.
101305.m: Fluorine-containing firefighting foam is an important source of PFAS in groundwater.

101306.q: Why are PFAS a problem for people and animals?
a: They build up in the body and are hardly excreted
They immediately break down into fluorine gas in the body
They are broken down into sugar in the stomach
101306.e: PFAS are hardly broken down and are excreted only very slowly. That is why some, such as PFOS, are banned or strongly restricted internationally.
101306.m: PFAS build up in living things.

101307.q: Which method is often used in waterworks to remove PFAS from drinking water?
101307.e: PFAS attach themselves to the large surface of activated carbon. Ion exchangers and reverse osmosis are also used, whereas boiling does not help.
101307.m: Activated carbon can filter PFAS out of drinking water.

101308.q: How many carbon atoms does perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) have?
101308.e: The word part “octan” stands for a chain of eight carbon atoms. Seven of them are perfluorinated, the eighth forms the carboxyl group.
101308.m: Perfluorooctanoic acid consists of a chain of eight carbon atoms.

101309.q: Which international agreement of 1987 governs the phase-out of CFCs?
101309.e: The Montreal Protocol commits countries to banning ozone-depleting substances step by step. It is considered one of the most successful environmental agreements.
101309.m: The 1987 Montreal Protocol brought about the worldwide phase-out of CFCs.

101310.q: Which three researchers received the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on the depletion of the ozone layer?
101310.e: In 1974 Molina and Rowland showed that CFCs release chlorine atoms in the stratosphere. Crutzen had previously described the role of nitrogen oxides in ozone depletion.
101310.m: Crutzen, Molina and Rowland explained how chemicals destroy the ozone layer.

101311.q: What splits the chlorine atoms off CFC molecules in the stratosphere?
101311.e: In the stratosphere, high-energy UV radiation hits the CFCs and splits the C-Cl bond. The free chlorine radicals then attack ozone.
101311.m: UV light releases chlorine radicals from CFCs in the stratosphere.

101312.q: Which reaction is the first step in the catalytic destruction of ozone by chlorine?
101312.e: A chlorine atom reacts with ozone to form chlorine monoxide and oxygen. ClO then reacts with an oxygen atom, which frees the chlorine atom again.
101312.m: In ozone destruction, a chlorine atom is freed again and again and so acts as a catalyst.

101313.q: Who developed CFCs as non-toxic refrigerants around 1930 and also brought leaded petrol onto the market?
101313.e: Thomas Midgley was looking for safe refrigerants for General Motors and found dichlorodifluoromethane. Both of his best-known inventions later turned out to be serious environmental problems.
101313.m: Thomas Midgley invented CFCs and leaded petrol.

101314.q: What is the molecular formula of the refrigerant R-12 (dichlorodifluoromethane)?
101314.e: The name says it all: a methane in which two H are replaced by Cl and two H by F. R-12 was one of the most widely used CFCs in fridges.
101314.m: Dichlorodifluoromethane carries two chlorine and two fluorine atoms on one carbon atom.

101315.q: Over which continent was the ozone hole first described in 1985?
101315.e: Researchers of the British Antarctic Survey led by Joseph Farman reported a sharp fall in ozone during the Antarctic spring in 1985. The cold and polar stratospheric clouds favour the depletion there.
101315.m: The ozone hole was discovered over Antarctica in 1985.

101316.q: Why were the hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) introduced as a replacement also restricted by the Kigali Amendment in 2016?
a: They destroy the ozone layer more than CFCs
101316.e: HFCs contain no chlorine and hardly harm the ozone layer. But many of them affect the climate thousands of times more strongly than CO₂.
101316.m: HFCs spare the ozone layer but heat up the climate strongly.

101317.q: According to common estimates, how many ozone molecules can a single chlorine atom in the stratosphere destroy before it is bound?
101317.e: Because the chlorine atom is released again and again in the reaction cycle, it acts as a catalyst. The chain only ends when it is bound in reservoir compounds such as HCl.
101317.m: One chlorine atom can destroy about a hundred thousand ozone molecules.

101318.q: What was the real name of the doctor who called himself Paracelsus?
101318.e: Paracelsus was called Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim. The nickname is often taken to mean “beyond Celsus”, after the Roman medical writer Celsus.
101318.m: Paracelsus's real name was Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim.

101319.q: What new approach to medicine did Paracelsus champion?
a: He used chemically prepared remedies made from minerals and metals
He cured illnesses only with prayers
He rejected all medicine on principle
He treated all patients only with bloodletting
101319.e: Paracelsus saw illnesses as chemical processes and used minerals and metals specifically as remedies. This approach is called iatrochemistry.
101319.m: Paracelsus put chemistry to work for medicine.

101320.q: Which famous principle of toxicology goes back to Paracelsus?
101320.e: Paracelsus realised that almost any substance is harmful in too large an amount, and that a poison can even heal in a small amount. This saying is still a principle of toxicology today.
101320.m: Whether a substance is poisonous depends on the amount.

101321.q: In which Swiss city was Paracelsus briefly town physician and professor in 1527?
101321.e: Paracelsus taught in Basel and gave his lectures in German instead of Latin. After quarrels with the scholars, he soon had to leave the city again.
101321.m: In 1527 Paracelsus worked as town physician in Basel.

101322.q: About which occupational diseases did Paracelsus write one of the first works of occupational medicine?
101322.e: In “On the Miners' Sickness and Other Diseases of Miners”, Paracelsus described lung diseases caused by dust and metal fumes. He knew mining from his youth in Villach.
101322.m: Paracelsus was an early describer of miners' lung diseases.

101323.q: Which metal is Paracelsus said to have given the name that is used today?
101323.e: Paracelsus used the name “zincum”, possibly because of its jagged crystals. The name later became generally accepted.
101323.m: The name zinc goes back to Paracelsus.

101324.q: Which word for a small earth spirit became known through a work by Paracelsus?
101324.e: In his book on elemental spirits, Paracelsus assigned beings to each element. He called the earth spirits gnomes and the water spirits undines.
101324.m: The word gnome comes from the writings of Paracelsus.

101325.q: Which opium tincture is traditionally attributed to Paracelsus?
101325.e: Paracelsus described a powerful painkiller containing opium, which he called laudanum. Later the name came to be used for alcoholic opium tinctures.
101325.m: Paracelsus is said to have introduced the opium preparation laudanum into medicine.

101326.q: What did Leopold Ružička receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for in 1939?
a: For work on polymethylenes and higher terpenes
101326.e: Ružička studied large ring compounds and terpenes, such as fragrances and natural substances. He shared the prize in 1939 with Adolf Butenandt.
101326.m: Leopold Ružička received the Nobel Prize in 1939 for his research on ring compounds and terpenes.

101327.q: Which present-day country did the ETH chemist Leopold Ružička come from?
101327.e: Ružička was born in 1887 in Vukovar, which then belonged to Austria-Hungary. He came to Zurich via Karlsruhe and became Swiss in 1917.
101327.m: Leopold Ružička came from present-day Croatia.

101328.q: How many carbon atoms does a triterpene built from six isoprene units contain?
101328.e: One isoprene unit has five carbon atoms. Six units give 6 · 5 = 30 carbon atoms.
101328.m: Terpenes are made of isoprene units with five carbon atoms each.

101329.q: What is the rule formulated by Ružička called, according to which terpenes are built from units of five carbon atoms?
101329.e: According to the biogenetic isoprene rule, terpenes form in living things by linking C₅ units. Ružička refined it in 1953.
101329.m: The isoprene rule explains how terpenes are built from five-carbon units.

101330.q: Which special feature did Ružička discover in musk fragrances?
a: They have very large carbon rings
They consist of short chains without a ring
101330.e: Muscone has a ring of 15 carbon atoms and civetone one of 17. Before this, such large rings were thought to be unstable.
101330.m: Ružička showed that musk fragrances have very large carbon rings.

101331.q: For which branch of industry was Ružička's research in Geneva particularly important?
101331.e: In the 1920s Ružička did research for a Geneva fragrance company that later became today's Firmenich. His work made artificial fragrances possible.
101331.m: Ružička's fragrance research shaped the Geneva perfume industry.

101332.q: What is Hermann Staudinger, Ružička's teacher, known for in chemistry?
a: He founded the chemistry of macromolecules
He developed the synthesis of ammonia
He drew up the periodic table
101332.e: Staudinger showed that plastics and many natural substances consist of huge chain molecules. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this in 1953.
101332.m: Hermann Staudinger is considered the father of polymer chemistry.

101333.q: At which university did the chemistry Nobel Prize winners Leopold Ružička and Vladimir Prelog do research?
101333.e: Ružička brought Prelog to ETH Zurich in 1941, where he later became his successor. Prelog received the Nobel Prize in 1975 for work on stereochemistry.
101333.m: Ružička and Prelog made ETH Zurich a centre of organic chemistry.

101334.q: Which processes in molecules does infrared radiation mainly excite in IR spectroscopy?
a: Electron transitions in the atomic nucleus
101334.e: Infrared light has the right energy to make bonds stretch and bend. Each vibration absorbs at a particular wavenumber.
101334.m: Infrared spectroscopy measures how bonds in molecules vibrate.

101335.q: In which range does the strong band of a C=O double bond typically appear in the IR spectrum?
101335.e: Carbonyl groups in ketones, aldehydes or carboxylic acids show a very intense band at around 1650 to 1750 cm⁻¹. It is one of the most striking bands in the IR spectrum.
101335.m: A strong band at around 1700 wavenumbers points to a carbonyl group.

101336.q: How does an alcohol O-H group with hydrogen bonding typically show up in the IR spectrum?
a: As a broad band at around 3200 to 3550 cm⁻¹
As a sharp band at around 1000 cm⁻¹
As a weak band at around 2200 cm⁻¹
As a double band at around 1600 cm⁻¹
101336.e: Hydrogen bonds lead to many slightly different O-H bond strengths. This produces a broad, intense band above 3000 cm⁻¹.
101336.m: A broad band above 3200 wavenumbers reveals an OH group.

101337.q: What is the region below about 1500 cm⁻¹ called, whose complex pattern of bands is unique to each molecule?
101337.e: Here many vibrations of the whole molecular framework overlap. By comparing with reference spectra, a substance can be clearly identified.
101337.m: The fingerprint region below 1500 wavenumbers is unique to each molecule.

101338.q: Which wavelength corresponds to a wavenumber of 2000 cm⁻¹?
101338.e: The wavelength is the reciprocal of the wavenumber: 1 / 2000 cm⁻¹ = 0.0005 cm. That is 5 µm.
101338.m: The wavelength is the reciprocal of the wavenumber.

101339.q: Which astronomer discovered infrared radiation in 1800 using thermometers behind a prism?
101339.e: Herschel noticed that a thermometer beyond the red light warmed up even more. He had detected invisible heat radiation.
101339.m: William Herschel discovered infrared radiation in 1800.

101340.q: What is IR spectroscopy mainly used for in the chemistry lab?
a: to identify functional groups in molecules
to determine the mass of atomic nuclei
to measure the pH of a solution
101340.e: Each functional group, such as C=O or O-H, absorbs infrared light at typical wavenumbers. So you can read from the spectrum which groups a molecule contains.
101340.m: IR spectroscopy reveals the functional groups of a molecule.

101341.q: How does the vibration frequency of a bond change when an atom is replaced by a heavier isotope?
101341.e: A bond vibrates rather like a spring with weights. A heavier atom vibrates more slowly with almost the same bond strength, so the IR band is at a lower wavenumber.

101442.e: Tropical rainforests grow near the equator, for example in South America, Africa and South East Asia.
101442.m: Tropical rainforests lie close to the equator.

101443.q: What is the weather usually like in the tropical rainforest?
101443.e: In the tropical rainforest the air is warm and very humid. Many plants like that.
101443.m: In the rainforest it is warm and humid.

101444.q: Which animal lives in the tropical rainforest?
101444.e: The sloth hangs slowly in the trees of the rainforest in South and Central America.
101444.m: The sloth lives in the trees of the rainforest.

101445.q: Which colourful bird with a very big beak lives in the rainforest?
101445.e: The toucan lives in the rainforests of South and Central America. Its huge beak is light and colourful.
101445.m: The toucan has a big, colourful beak.

101446.q: Which big spotted wild cat prowls through the South American rainforest?
101446.e: The jaguar is the biggest wild cat in America. It lives in the rainforest and can even swim well.
101446.m: The jaguar lives in the rainforest of South America.

101447.q: Where is it darkest in the tropical rainforest?
101447.e: The thick leaves at the top block almost all the sunlight. That is why it is dark down on the ground.
101447.m: It is dark on the floor of the rainforest.

101448.q: Which small, brightly coloured frogs in the rainforest are poisonous?
101448.e: Poison dart frogs live in the rainforests of South and Central America. Their bright colours warn enemies of the poison in their skin.
101448.m: Colourful poison dart frogs are poisonous.

101449.q: Which monkey can hold on to branches with its tail?
101449.e: The spider monkey uses its long tail like a fifth hand. Great apes such as gorillas have no tail at all.
101449.m: The spider monkey holds on with its tail.

101450.q: What do lianas climb up in the rainforest?
101450.e: Lianas take root in the ground and climb up tree trunks. The trees serve as their support.

101451.q: Where do lianas want to get to when they climb upwards?
101451.e: Down in the rainforest it is dark. Lianas climb up to get their leaves into the sunlight.
101451.m: Lianas climb up towards the light.

101452.q: Which plant from our woods also climbs like a liana?
101452.e: There are lianas in Switzerland too. Ivy climbs up trees and walls with little clinging roots.
101452.m: Ivy is a liana from our woods.

101453.q: Which character swings through the jungle on lianas in stories?
101453.e: Tarzan is a famous character from books and films. He grows up in the jungle and swings on lianas.
101453.m: Tarzan swings through the jungle on lianas.

101454.q: What do lianas need to grow tall?
101454.e: Lianas have no thick, strong trunk. They need a support such as a tree to hold on to.
101454.m: Lianas need a support to climb.

101455.q: Which animals like to use lianas as a path between the trees?
101455.e: Monkeys climb along lianas and get from tree to tree without having to go down to the ground.

101456.q: Which plant with grapes is also a liana?
101456.e: The grapevine is a climbing plant. It holds on with tendrils and bears grapes.
101456.m: The grapevine is a climbing plant.

101457.e: Rainforest giants are the tallest trees in the rainforest. They are often very old.
101457.m: A rainforest giant is a huge tree in the rainforest.

101458.q: Which flowers often grow high up on the branches of rainforest giants?
101458.e: In the rainforest many orchids grow not in the ground but on the branches of tall trees. There they get more light.
101458.m: In the rainforest many orchids grow on tree branches.

101459.q: What do many rainforest giants use to support themselves on the ground?
101459.e: Buttress roots are wide, flat roots like walls on the trunk. They give the tall trees a firm hold.
101459.m: Buttress roots hold rainforest giants firm.

101460.q: Which rainforest giant in the Amazon region produces edible nuts?
101460.e: The Brazil nut tree grows up to about 50 metres tall. Its nuts grow in hard capsules.
101460.m: Brazil nuts grow on a rainforest giant.

101461.q: Which rainforest giant has seeds with soft fluff that used to be stuffed into pillows?
101461.e: The kapok tree is a rainforest giant. The soft fibres from its fruits are called kapok.
101461.m: The kapok tree provides soft fibres.

101462.q: What happens when a rainforest giant falls over?
101462.e: Sunlight falls on the ground through the gap in the canopy. Now young trees can grow quickly.
101462.m: A fallen tree brings light to the ground.

101463.q: Which big bird of prey builds its nest high up in rainforest giants?
101463.e: The harpy eagle is a mighty bird of prey from the rainforest. It builds its nest in the crowns of very tall trees.
101463.m: The harpy eagle nests in rainforest giants.

101464.q: On which continent does the Amazon flow?
101464.e: The Amazon flows through South America, mainly through Peru and Brazil.
101464.m: The Amazon flows in South America.

101465.e: The Amazon is a huge river. The largest rainforest on Earth grows around it.
101465.m: The Amazon is a big river.

101466.q: In which country is most of the Amazon rainforest?
101466.e: About 60 per cent of the Amazon rainforest lies in Brazil.
101466.m: Most of the Amazon rainforest lies in Brazil.

101467.q: Into which ocean does the Amazon flow?
101467.e: The Amazon flows into the Atlantic Ocean on the coast of Brazil.
101467.m: The Amazon flows into the Atlantic.

101468.q: What colour are many river dolphins in the Amazon?
101468.e: The Amazon river dolphin often turns pink with age. That is why it is also called the pink river dolphin.
101468.m: Pink dolphins live in the Amazon.

101469.q: Which plant on the Amazon has round leaves that grow more than two metres wide?
101469.e: The giant water lily grows in the Amazon region. Its floating leaves can grow up to about three metres wide.
101469.m: The giant water lily has huge round leaves.

101470.q: Which river in the world carries the most water?
101470.e: No other river carries as much water into the sea as the Amazon.
101470.m: The Amazon is the river with the most water in the world.

101471.q: What is almost completely missing in a desert?
101471.e: In a desert it rains very rarely. That is why only a few plants grow there.
101471.m: It rains very little in the desert.

101472.q: Which desert animal has a hump on its back?
101472.e: The dromedary has one hump. It stores fat in it as a reserve.

101473.q: What happens in many deserts at night?
101473.e: In the daytime it is hot, but at night the desert cools down a lot. There are no clouds to hold the warmth in.
101473.m: It can get cold in the desert at night.

101474.q: What is a hill of sand shaped by the wind called?
101474.e: The wind blows sand together into hills. These hills of sand are called dunes.
101474.m: A dune is a hill of sand.

101475.q: Which area also counts as a desert because it has very little precipitation?
101475.e: A desert does not have to be hot. So little precipitation falls in Antarctica that it counts as a cold desert.

101476.q: Which animal with a venomous sting on its tail lives in deserts?
101476.e: Scorpions often live in deserts. There is a venomous sting at the end of their tail.
101476.m: The scorpion has a sting on its tail.

101477.q: Where does the water in an oasis usually come from?
101477.e: There is often groundwater under the desert. In the oasis it comes out as a spring or is drawn from wells.
101477.m: Oases usually get their water from the ground.

101478.q: Why do caravans stop at oases?
101478.e: There is hardly any water in the desert. The people and animals of a caravan drink at the oasis and fill up their supplies.
101478.m: Travellers get water at the oasis.

101479.q: What is a group of travellers with camels in the desert called?
101479.e: A caravan travels through the desert with camels and goods, often from oasis to oasis.
101479.m: A caravan travels through the desert with camels.

101480.q: What is a mirage in the desert?
a: A picture that is not real
101480.e: In great heat the air reflects things. Some travellers then think they see water in the distance, but it is not there at all.
101480.m: A mirage is an optical illusion.

101481.q: How much water can a thirsty dromedary drink at an oasis in one go?
101481.e: A dromedary can go a very long time without water. When it finds water, it drinks a great deal in a few minutes, up to about 100 litres.
101481.m: A thirsty dromedary can drink a lot of water in one go.

101482.q: In which country is the famous Siwa Oasis?
101482.e: Siwa lies in the desert in the west of Egypt, near the border with Libya.
101482.m: The Siwa Oasis is in Egypt.

101483.q: What do the palms in the oasis give people?
101483.e: The palms protect against the hot sun. Other plants also grow better under them.
101483.m: Palms give shade in the oasis.

101484.q: What do people use the long leaves of the date palm for?
101484.e: People weave baskets and mats from the leaves of the date palm. They also use them to cover roofs.
101484.m: You can weave baskets from palm leaves.

101485.q: Where do date palms like to grow?
101485.e: Date palms love heat. But they need water in the ground, for example in an oasis.
101485.m: Date palms grow in hot areas.

101486.q: How do dates hang on the palm?
101486.e: Dates grow in big, heavy bunches at the top under the leaves.
101486.m: Dates hang in bunches on the palm.

101487.q: What is often done with dates so that they keep for a long time?
101487.e: Dried dates keep for a long time. That is how we know them from the shops in Switzerland too.
101487.m: Dried dates keep for a long time.

101488.e: Inside every date there is a hard, long stone. A new palm can grow from it.
101488.m: There is a hard stone inside a date.

101489.q: What do succulents store in their thick leaves or stems?
101489.e: Succulents are plants that store water. That way they survive long dry periods.

101490.q: Which of these plants is a succulent?
101490.e: The cactus stores water in its thick stem. That is why it is a succulent.

101491.q: What do many cacti have instead of green leaves?
101491.e: In many cacti the leaves have turned into spines. The spines protect against animals and lose hardly any water.
101491.m: Cacti have spines instead of leaves.

101492.q: Where do wild cacti like to grow best?
a: Where it is hot and dry
101492.e: Cacti store water in their thick stem. That is why they can live in hot, dry areas such as deserts.
101492.m: Cacti live where it is hot and dry.

101493.q: Which succulent is often found in skin creams?
101493.e: Aloe vera has thick leaves full of gel. This gel is often used in creams.
101493.m: Aloe vera has leaves full of gel.

101494.q: Which succulent also grows on rocks in the Swiss Alps?
101494.e: The houseleek has thick leaves in rosettes. It grows on dry, sunny rocks, in the Alps too.
101494.m: The houseleek grows on rocks in the Alps.

101495.q: On which continent do most cacti grow wild?
101495.e: Almost all cacti come from America, for example from Mexico and the USA. People later planted them on other continents.

101496.q: How often do you need to water a succulent indoors?
101496.e: Succulents need little water. Too much water makes their roots rot.

101497.q: Why do hardly any trees grow in the tundra?
101497.e: In the tundra it is very cold for a long time, and the summer is short. Trees cannot grow there.
101497.m: The tundra is too cold for trees.

101498.q: Which animals roam the tundra in big herds?
101498.e: Reindeer move through the tundra in big herds. In North America they are called caribou.

101499.q: What mainly grows in the tundra?
101499.e: Low plants such as mosses, lichens, grasses and dwarf shrubs grow in the tundra.
101499.m: Mosses and lichens grow in the tundra.

101500.q: Which animal with a white winter coat lives in the tundra?
101500.e: The Arctic fox has a white coat in winter. That way it is well camouflaged in the snow.
101500.m: The Arctic fox is white in winter.

101501.q: What happens in summer in the far north?
101501.e: In summer the sun does not set for days in the far north. This is called the midnight sun.
101501.m: In summer the midnight sun shines in the far north.

101502.q: Which small animal with a bushy tail gets seeds out of cones in the taiga?
101502.e: The squirrel lives in coniferous forests such as the taiga. It gnaws cones open and eats the seeds inside.
101502.m: The squirrel likes eating seeds from cones.

101503.q: Which big animal with broad, flat antlers lives in the taiga?
101503.e: The elk, called moose in North America, is the biggest deer in the world. The males have broad, flat antlers.
101503.m: The elk lives in the taiga.

101504.q: In which country is a huge part of the taiga?
101504.e: In Siberia in Russia, the taiga stretches for thousands of kilometres.
101504.m: A large part of the taiga is in Russia.

101505.q: Which bear lives in the forests of the taiga?
101505.e: The brown bear lives in the forests of the taiga. In winter it rests in a cave.
101505.m: The brown bear lives in the taiga.

101506.q: Which big wild cat lives in the taiga in eastern Russia?
101506.e: The Siberian tiger, also called the Amur tiger, lives in the forests of eastern Russia.
101506.m: The Siberian tiger lives in the taiga.

101507.q: Which water can mangroves cope with?
101507.e: Most plants die in salt water. Mangroves can live with it.

101508.e: At high tide the sea rises and floods the mangroves. At low tide the ground dries out again.
101508.m: At high tide mangroves stand in the sea.

101509.q: Which monkey with a very big nose lives in mangroves on Borneo?
101509.e: The proboscis monkey lives on the island of Borneo in mangroves and forests along rivers. It can swim well.
101509.m: The proboscis monkey lives in the mangroves of Borneo.

101510.q: Which crab waves a big claw in the mangroves?
101510.e: In fiddler crabs, the male has one very big claw. It waves with it.
101510.m: The fiddler crab waves its big claw.

101511.q: What mainly grows in the savannah?
101511.e: A savannah is a wide grassland with scattered trees and bushes.
101511.m: A lot of grass grows in the savannah.

101512.q: Which animal with a long neck eats leaves from tall trees in the savannah?
101512.e: With its long neck the giraffe reaches leaves high up in the trees.
101512.m: The giraffe has a long neck.

101513.q: Which tree with a very thick trunk grows in the African savannah?
101513.e: The baobab, also called the monkey bread tree, stores water in its thick trunk.
101513.m: The baobab has a very thick trunk.

101514.q: Which striped animals live in herds in the savannah?
101514.e: Zebras have black and white stripes and live in herds in the African savannah.
101514.m: Zebras live in herds in the savannah.

101515.q: Which wild cat is the fastest land animal and lives in the savannah?
101515.e: For a short time the cheetah can run at over 90 kilometres per hour.
101515.m: The cheetah is the fastest land animal.

101516.q: Which two seasons are there in the savannah?
101516.e: In the savannah a rainy season and a dry season take turns.
101516.m: In the savannah there is a rainy season and a dry season.

101517.q: Which tree with a flat, umbrella-shaped crown is typical of the savannah?
101517.e: The umbrella thorn acacia has a wide, flat crown like an umbrella. Giraffes like eating its leaves.
101517.m: The umbrella thorn acacia looks like an umbrella.

101518.q: Which big bird that cannot fly lives in the African savannah?
101518.e: The ostrich is the biggest bird in the world. It cannot fly, but it can run very fast. The emu lives in Australia.
101518.m: The ostrich is the biggest bird.

101519.q: Which largest land animal lives in the African savannah?
101519.e: The African elephant is the biggest animal that lives on land.
101519.m: The elephant is the biggest land animal.

101520.q: Which country did the explorer Alexander von Humboldt come from?
101520.e: Alexander von Humboldt was born in Berlin in 1769. He became one of the most famous naturalists.
101520.m: Alexander von Humboldt came from Berlin.

101521.q: Which part of the world did Humboldt explore on his great journey from 1799?
101521.e: From 1799 to 1804 Humboldt travelled through South and Central America. He studied plants, animals, mountains and rivers.

101522.q: Which animal is named after Alexander von Humboldt?
101522.e: The Humboldt penguin lives on the coasts of Peru and Chile. It is named after the explorer.
101522.m: The Humboldt penguin is named after the explorer.

101523.q: Which high volcano in Ecuador did Humboldt try to climb in 1802?
101523.e: In 1802 Humboldt climbed to over 5,000 metres on Chimborazo. Hardly anyone had got that high at the time.

101524.q: Which continent did Alexander von Humboldt explore on his great journey from 1799?
101524.e: From 1799 Humboldt spent five years travelling through South and Central America. He studied rivers, mountains, plants and animals.

101525.q: Which cold ocean current off South America is named after Humboldt?
101525.e: The Humboldt Current brings cold water to the coasts of Chile and Peru. Humboldt measured its temperature.
101525.m: The Humboldt Current is a cold ocean current.

101526.q: What did Humboldt and his companion collect in large numbers on the journey?
101526.e: They collected tens of thousands of dried plants. Many of them were not yet known in Europe.
101526.m: Humboldt collected a great many plants.

101527.q: What did Alexander von Humboldt mainly do on his travels?
101527.e: Humboldt was a naturalist. He measured, collected and described plants, animals, mountains and the weather.

101528.e: James Cook was a captain and seafarer. He led great voyages of discovery by ship.
101528.m: James Cook was the captain of a ship.

101529.q: On the coast of which continent did Cook land in 1770?
101529.e: In 1770 Cook reached the east coast of Australia and drew it on maps.

101530.q: Which island country did James Cook sail around in 1769 and map exactly?
101530.e: Cook sailed around New Zealand in 1769 and 1770. He showed that it is made up of two large islands.
101530.m: Cook drew an exact map of New Zealand.

101531.q: How many great voyages of discovery did James Cook make?
101531.e: Cook led three great voyages to the Pacific between 1768 and 1779.
101531.m: James Cook made three great voyages of discovery.

101532.q: What did Cook make his sailors eat so that they would not get scurvy?
101532.e: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C. Cook took lots of sauerkraut on board.

101533.q: Which line in the cold south did Cook become the first to cross by ship in 1773?
101533.e: On his second voyage in 1773, Cook was the first to sail across the Antarctic Circle. But he never actually saw Antarctica itself.
101533.m: Cook was the first to sail across the Antarctic Circle.

101535.q: On which continent did Darwin spend the longest time on land during the Beagle voyage?
101535.e: The Beagle mainly surveyed the coasts of South America. Darwin made many long trips inland there.

101536.q: In which year did Darwin set off on the Beagle?
101536.e: The Beagle left the harbour of Plymouth in England on 27 December 1831.

101537.q: What was Darwin's job on the Beagle?
101537.e: Darwin was on board as a naturalist. He observed animals, plants and rocks.
101537.m: Darwin was the naturalist on the Beagle.

101538.q: What did Darwin often suffer from on the ship?
101538.e: Darwin often felt sick on the rocking ship. That is why he went ashore as often as he could.
101538.m: Darwin was often seasick on the ship.

101539.q: Which famous theory did Darwin develop after his voyage?
101539.e: Darwin explained that living things change over a very long time. This is called evolution.
101539.m: Darwin developed the theory of evolution.

101540.q: How old was Darwin when the Beagle voyage began?
101540.e: Darwin was born in February 1809. When the Beagle set sail at the end of 1831, he was a young man of 22.
101540.m: Darwin was still a young man when the ship set sail.

101541.q: Among other things, what did Darwin collect on his travels?
101541.e: In South America Darwin dug up bones of extinct giant animals. Such remains turned to stone are called fossils.

101542.q: Which lizard on the Galápagos swims in the sea and eats seaweed?
101542.e: The marine iguana dives in the sea for seaweed. It lives only on the Galápagos Islands.
101542.m: The marine iguana swims in the sea.

101543.q: Which bird with bright blue feet lives on the Galápagos?
101543.e: The blue-footed booby has light blue feet. It proudly shows them off in its courtship dance.
101543.m: The blue-footed booby has blue feet.

101544.q: Which small birds on the Galápagos are named after Darwin?
101544.e: Darwin's finches have different beaks depending on the island. Later they helped people understand how species develop.
101544.m: Darwin's finches live on the Galápagos.

101545.q: Which animal lives on the Galápagos, even though you would rather expect it in cold places?
101545.e: The Galápagos penguin lives almost on the equator. Cold sea water makes this possible.
101545.m: Penguins live on the Galápagos, right by the equator.

101546.q: In which year did Darwin visit the Galápagos Islands?
101546.e: The Beagle reached the Galápagos Islands in September 1835. Darwin stayed for about five weeks.
101546.m: Darwin was on the Galápagos in 1835.

101547.q: Since 1978, the Galápagos Islands have been on which list because of their nature?
101547.e: In 1978 the Galápagos Islands were among the very first sites added to the UNESCO World Heritage list.
101547.m: The Galápagos Islands are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

101548.q: How old can Galápagos giant tortoises get?
101548.e: Giant tortoises get very old. Many live for over 100 years.
101548.m: Giant tortoises can live for over 100 years.

101549.q: What do Galápagos giant tortoises eat?
101549.e: Giant tortoises eat grasses, leaves and even cacti.

101550.q: What are the Galápagos Islands named after?
101550.e: Galápago is an old Spanish word for tortoise. So the islands are named after the giant tortoises.
101550.m: The Galápagos Islands are named after tortoises.

101551.q: How heavy can Galápagos giant tortoises get?
101551.e: Large males can weigh over 200 kilograms. That is about as heavy as three adults together.

101552.q: Why was the giant tortoise Lonesome George famous?
a: He was the last of his kind
He was the biggest tortoise in the world
He lived in a zoo in Europe
101552.e: Lonesome George was the last giant tortoise from the island of Pinta. He died in 2012.
101552.m: Lonesome George was the last of his kind.

101553.q: Why did sailors in the past take giant tortoises on board?
101553.e: Giant tortoises can survive a long time without food. So sailors took them along as a supply of fresh meat. Many animals were lost this way.
101553.m: In the past sailors hunted many giant tortoises.

101554.q: Where does a giant tortoise go when there is danger?
101554.e: The tortoise pulls its head and legs back into its hard shell.

101555.q: How does a giant tortoise move?
101555.e: Giant tortoises walk slowly. They manage less than one kilometre per hour.

101556.q: On which river did Humboldt travel through the rainforest by canoe?
101556.e: In 1800 Humboldt paddled up the Orinoco in Venezuela by canoe.

101557.q: What do explorers use to cut a path through the thick rainforest?
101557.e: A machete is a long bush knife. You use it to cut away branches and plants.
101557.m: You cut a path with a machete.

101558.q: Which annoying insects bite especially often in the rainforest?
101558.e: In the warm, damp rainforest there are huge numbers of mosquitoes. They bite day and night.
101558.m: Lots of mosquitoes bite in the rainforest.

101559.q: How do scientists today get up into the treetops of the rainforest?
101559.e: Scientists climb up with ropes and harnesses. Sometimes they also use rope bridges or cranes.
101559.m: Scientists climb into the treetops with ropes.

101560.q: Why did explorers in the Amazon rainforest mostly travel by boat?
101560.e: The forest is very thick. Rivers were the easiest routes through the rainforest.
101560.m: Rivers are routes through the rainforest.

101561.q: The sap of some rainforest trees is used to make a material for bicycle tyres and wellies. Which one?
101561.e: The rubber tree from the Amazon has a white milky sap. Rubber is made from it.
101561.m: Rubber comes from the rubber tree of the rainforest.

101562.q: What do scientists keep discovering in the rainforest even today?
101562.e: So many species live in the rainforest that scientists find new animals and plants every year.
101562.m: There are still unknown species in the rainforest.

101563.q: Which device helps explorers in a thick forest find the direction?
101563.e: The needle of a compass points north. That way you don't lose your direction.

101564.q: What do you call a journey to explore an unknown area?
101564.e: An expedition is a planned journey of exploration, for example into the rainforest.
101564.m: A journey of exploration is called an expedition.

101565.q: Where did Jacques Piccard dive in 1960?
101565.e: The Mariana Trench in the Pacific is the deepest place in the oceans. In 1960 Piccard dived all the way to its bottom.
101565.m: Jacques Piccard dived to the deepest place in the sea.

101566.q: How deep did Jacques Piccard dive in 1960?
101566.e: The Trieste reached a depth of almost 11,000 metres. That is deeper than Mount Everest is high.

101567.q: In what did Auguste Piccard, the father of Jacques Piccard, fly high into the sky?
101567.e: In 1931 Auguste Piccard flew higher in a balloon than any person before him. Later he also built a submersible.
101567.m: Auguste Piccard flew in a balloon.

101568.q: How many people sat in Jacques Piccard's submersible in 1960?
101568.e: Jacques Piccard and the American Don Walsh sat together in the cramped steel sphere of the Trieste.
101568.m: Piccard dived into the Mariana Trench with one other person.

101569.q: What is it like at the bottom of the Mariana Trench?
101569.e: No sunlight reaches that deep into the sea. The water down there is only a few degrees warm.
101569.m: The deep sea is dark and cold.

101570.q: Which country did the deep-sea explorer Jacques Piccard come from?
101570.e: Jacques Piccard was born in Brussels, but he was Swiss. He lived in French-speaking Switzerland.

101571.q: How long did the Trieste stay at the deepest point in 1960?
101571.e: The descent took almost five hours. The two men stayed on the bottom for only about 20 minutes.
101571.m: The Trieste stayed only a short time at the deepest point.

101572.e: Bertrand Piccard comes from a family of explorers. His father was the deep-sea explorer Jacques Piccard.
101572.m: Bertrand Piccard is the son of Jacques Piccard.

101573.q: What did Bertrand Piccard achieve with a balloon in 1999?
a: Flying round the Earth without stopping
101573.e: In 1999 Bertrand Piccard was one of the first to fly a balloon round the whole Earth without landing.
101573.m: Bertrand Piccard flew round the Earth in a balloon.

101574.q: In which aircraft did Bertrand Piccard fly round the Earth in 2016 using only solar energy?
101574.e: The Solar Impulse 2 aircraft had huge wings full of solar cells and flew without any fuel. Piccard and André Borschberg took turns at the controls.
101574.m: Solar Impulse flew round the world using only solar energy.

101575.q: How long did Bertrand Piccard's balloon flight round the world last?
101575.e: In March 1999 the balloon travelled for nearly 20 days without stopping.
101575.m: The balloon flight round the world lasted about 20 days.

101576.q: Roughly how long did Bertrand Piccard's balloon flight round the Earth in 1999 take?
101576.e: The balloon travelled for almost 20 days without landing. In the end it came down in the desert in Egypt.
101576.m: The balloon flight round the Earth took about three weeks.

101577.q: In which city was Bertrand Piccard born in 1958?
101577.e: Bertrand Piccard was born in 1958 in Lausanne on Lake Geneva.

101578.q: In what did Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg fly round the world in 2015 and 2016?
101578.e: The Solar Impulse 2 aircraft flew round the world using only solar energy. Solar cells on the wings charged the batteries.
101578.m: Bertrand Piccard flew round the world in a solar plane.

101579.q: What powered the Solar Impulse aircraft?
101579.e: There were lots of solar cells on the wings. They turned sunlight into electricity, and batteries stored electricity for the night.
101579.m: Solar Impulse flew on solar energy.

101580.q: When did Solar Impulse 2 fly round the world?
101580.e: The round-the-world flight began in March 2015 and ended in July 2016.
101580.m: Solar Impulse 2 flew round the world in 2015 and 2016.

101581.q: How many pilots fitted in the cockpit of Solar Impulse 2?
101581.e: The cockpit was as small as a phone box. So the pilots flew alone and took turns.
101581.m: Only one pilot sat in the cockpit at a time.

101582.q: Which Swiss man flew round the world in Solar Impulse 2?
101582.e: Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg took turns flying Solar Impulse 2 round the world. Claude Nicollier and Marco Sieber are astronauts, and Jacques Piccard dived into the deep sea.
101582.m: Bertrand Piccard flew round the world in Solar Impulse.

101583.q: How wide were the wings of Solar Impulse 2?
101583.e: The wings were about 72 metres wide, which is wider than those of a jumbo jet.
101583.m: Solar Impulse 2 had very wide wings.

101584.q: Roughly how heavy was Solar Impulse 2?
a: About as heavy as a car
As heavy as a jumbo jet
101584.e: Solar Impulse 2 weighed only about 2.3 tonnes. That is roughly as much as a large car.

101585.q: How long did the longest non-stop flight from Japan to Hawaii take?
101585.e: The pilot flew almost 118 hours across the Pacific without landing. That is almost five days.
101585.m: The longest flight took almost five days.

101586.q: Which city did the traveller Ida Pfeiffer come from?
101586.e: Ida Pfeiffer was born in Vienna in 1797.

101587.q: What made Ida Pfeiffer from Vienna famous in the 19th century?
a: She travelled round the world alone
She was the first to reach the North Pole
She was the first to climb the Matterhorn
She built the first steam engine
101587.e: Ida Pfeiffer was one of the first women to travel all the way round the world alone.
101587.m: Ida Pfeiffer travelled round the world alone as a woman.

101588.q: How many times did Ida Pfeiffer travel round the world?
101588.e: Between 1846 and 1855 Ida Pfeiffer made two journeys round the world.
101588.m: Ida Pfeiffer travelled round the world twice.

101589.q: How did Ida Pfeiffer earn money for her travels?
101589.e: She wrote books about her travels. With the money she paid for her next journey.
101589.m: Ida Pfeiffer wrote books about her travels.

101590.q: What did Ida Pfeiffer collect on her travels for museums?
101590.e: She brought back beetles, butterflies, plants and stones. Museums bought many of them from her.
101590.m: Ida Pfeiffer collected insects and plants.

101591.q: Which cold island in the north did Ida Pfeiffer visit in 1845?
101591.e: In 1845 Ida Pfeiffer travelled to Iceland and wrote a book about it.
101591.m: Ida Pfeiffer travelled to Iceland in 1845.

101592.q: Roughly how old was Ida Pfeiffer when her first big journey began?
101592.e: In 1842 she started with a journey to the Holy Land. Her children were already grown up by then.
101592.m: Ida Pfeiffer only started travelling late in life.

101593.q: Who built the first hot-air balloon that carried people?
101593.e: The French Montgolfier brothers built the first large hot-air balloons.
101593.m: The Montgolfier brothers invented the hot-air balloon.

101594.q: In which year did people fly in a hot-air balloon for the first time?
101594.e: On 21 November 1783, two men flew in a hot-air balloon in Paris for the first time.
101594.m: The first balloon flight with people was in 1783.

101595.q: Which animals were the first passengers to fly in a balloon?
a: A sheep, a duck and a cockerel
A dog, a cat and a mouse
A horse, a cow and a goat
A monkey, a parrot and a hare
101595.e: Before people flew, the balloon was tested with a sheep, a duck and a cockerel. All three survived the flight.
101595.m: A sheep, a duck and a cockerel were the first to fly in a balloon.

101596.q: What is used to heat the air in a hot-air balloon today?
101596.e: A burner under the opening of the balloon burns gas. The flame heats the air inside the envelope.
101596.m: A gas burner heats the air in the balloon.

101597.q: What do the passengers of a hot-air balloon stand in?
101597.e: The passengers stand in a sturdy wicker basket under the balloon.

101598.q: What decides which direction a hot-air balloon flies in?
101598.e: You can't steer a hot-air balloon. The pilot goes up or down to find a wind blowing in the right direction.
101598.m: A hot-air balloon flies with the wind.

101599.q: When do hot-air balloons like to fly best?
101599.e: Early in the morning and in the evening the air is usually calm. Then a balloon flight is safe.
101599.m: Balloons like to take off on calm mornings.

101600.q: What do you write in a travel diary?
a: Things that happen on the trip
101600.e: In a travel diary you record what you see and experience on a journey.
101600.m: You write your experiences in a travel diary.

101601.q: Why did explorers keep a diary on their journeys?
101601.e: Explorers wrote down what they found and measured. That way nothing was lost and others could learn from it later.
101601.m: A diary helps you not to forget discoveries.

101602.q: What is a ship's diary called?
101602.e: In the logbook the crew notes the course, the weather and important events at sea.
101602.m: A ship's diary is called a logbook.

101603.q: Apart from writing, what do many travellers put in their travel diary?
101603.e: Many travellers draw animals, plants and landscapes in their diary.
101603.m: A travel diary can also contain drawings.

101604.q: What do people often write above each entry in a travel diary?
101604.e: With the date and place you know later exactly when and where something happened.
101604.m: Each entry gets a date and a place.

101605.q: What did explorers 250 years ago use to write in their diaries?
101605.e: Back then there were no ballpoint pens or felt-tips. People dipped a quill into ink.
101605.m: In the past people wrote with a quill and ink.

101606.q: What did Darwin's travel diary later become?
101606.e: Darwin's account of the voyage was printed as a book. Many people read it.
101606.m: Darwin's travel account became a book.

101607.q: What do you call a single piece of writing in a diary?
101607.e: Every day, or after every experience, you write a new entry in the diary.
101607.m: A piece of writing in a diary is called an entry.

101608.q: Which parts of the body does a sun hat with a wide brim protect?
101608.e: The wide brim casts shade on the face, ears and neck. The hat itself covers the head.
101608.m: A hat with a wide brim protects your head, face and neck.

101609.q: What is the rim of a hat called?
101609.e: The rim that sticks out from a hat is called the brim. The wider the brim, the more shade it gives.
101609.m: The rim of a hat is called the brim.

101610.q: Which colour of hat gets less hot in the sun?
101610.e: Light colours reflect a lot of sunlight. Dark colours absorb the light and get hot.
101610.m: Light clothes and hats stay cooler in the sun.

101611.q: What does a cap with neck protection have at the back?
a: A piece of fabric over the neck
101611.e: With this cap, a piece of fabric hangs down at the back. It protects the neck from sunburn.
101611.m: Neck protection covers the neck with fabric.

101612.q: Why should small children wear a hat in the sun?
a: Their head is sensitive to the sun
101612.e: Children's scalps are often not well covered by hair, and their skin is sensitive. A hat protects against sunburn and overheating.
101612.m: Children always wear a hat in the sun.

a: A hat made of woven straw
101613.e: Straw hats are woven from dried stalks. They are light and let air through.
101613.m: A straw hat is light and airy.

101614.q: When is a sun hat most important?
a: At midday when it is very sunny
Early in the morning in bed
101614.e: At midday, the sun is highest and strongest. That is when your head needs the most protection.
101614.m: At midday, your head needs the most sun protection.

101615.q: What is the strap under the chin on some sun hats for?
a: So the wind does not blow the hat away
101615.e: The chin strap holds the hat firmly on your head. That way it stays on even in the wind or while you play.
101615.m: A chin strap holds your hat on in the wind.

101616.q: Can we see UV rays with our eyes?
101616.e: UV rays are a part of sunlight that our eyes cannot see. Even so, they affect our skin and eyes.
101616.m: UV rays are invisible, but they still have an effect.

101617.q: Where does most of the UV radiation that reaches us come from?
101617.e: As well as light and warmth, the sun also sends out UV rays. It is our biggest source of UV.
101617.m: Most UV radiation comes from the sun.

101618.q: What can too much UV radiation do to your skin?
a: Cause a gap in your teeth
101618.e: UV rays damage the skin. It turns red, gets hot and hurts.
101618.m: Too much UV radiation causes sunburn.

101619.q: Does UV radiation also get through clouds?
101619.e: Clouds only block part of the UV radiation. That is why you can get sunburnt on cloudy days too.
101619.m: Even when it is cloudy, the sun can burn your skin.

a: In the shade of a house
101620.e: In the mountains, the layer of air above us is thinner. It blocks less UV radiation.
101620.m: The sun is stronger in the mountains than in the valley.

101621.q: Which layer high up in the air blocks a lot of UV radiation?
101621.e: The ozone layer lies high above the Earth. It absorbs a large part of the dangerous UV radiation.
101621.m: The ozone layer protects us from a lot of UV radiation.

101622.q: Why does your skin go brown in summer?
a: It is protecting itself from UV rays
101622.e: In the sun, the skin makes more dark pigment. This protects a little against UV rays, but not enough.
101622.m: Tanned skin is a sign that your skin is defending itself.

101623.q: Apart from the skin, which parts of the body can UV rays also damage?
101623.e: UV rays can irritate the eyes and damage them over time. Good sunglasses help.
101623.m: Your eyes also need protection from UV rays.

a: A lot of sun on your head and neck
101624.e: If the sun shines for a long time on an unprotected head and neck, the brain gets irritated. This is called sunstroke.
101624.m: Sunstroke comes from too much sun on your head.

101625.q: What is a typical sign of sunstroke?
101625.e: With sunstroke, your head often hurts. You may also feel dizzy and sick and have a red, hot head.
101625.m: A headache after a lot of sun can be sunstroke.

101626.q: What do you do first if someone has sunstroke?
a: Carry on playing in the sun
101626.e: The person must get out of the sun at once. In the shade, the head can recover.
101626.m: With sunstroke, go into the shade at once.

101627.q: What do you cool the head with if someone has sunstroke?
101627.e: Cool, wet cloths on the head and neck help. They take away heat.
101627.m: Cool cloths help a hot head.

101628.q: How does the head often feel with sunstroke?
101628.e: With sunstroke, the head is usually hot and red. The rest of the body, however, can be normally warm.
101628.m: A hot, red head fits with sunstroke.

101629.e: A hat or cap keeps the sun off your head. That way the brain does not overheat.
101629.m: A hat is the best protection against sunstroke.

101630.q: How should a person with sunstroke lie?
a: On their tummy in the sun
101630.e: You raise the upper body and head a little. That takes pressure off the head.
101630.m: With sunstroke, the head lies a little higher.

101631.q: What should someone with sunstroke drink?
101631.e: If the person is conscious, they may drink water in sips. That replaces the fluid they have lost.
101631.m: After a lot of sun, drink water in small sips.

a: The whole body gets too hot
101632.e: With heatstroke, the body can no longer get rid of its heat. The body temperature rises dangerously high.
101632.m: Heatstroke means the whole body overheats.

101633.e: Heatstroke can be life-threatening. You must get help immediately.

101634.q: Where must you never leave children and animals alone in summer?
a: In the garden in the shade
At the swimming pool with supervision
101634.e: A car in the sun gets very hot inside very quickly. That can lead to heatstroke.
101634.m: In summer, nobody stays alone in a parked car.

101635.q: What helps against heatstroke on hot days?
101635.e: If you drink enough, you can sweat and cool your body that way. That helps prevent heatstroke.
101635.m: On hot days, drink lots of water.

101636.q: When should you not do tiring sport on hot days?
a: At midday and in the afternoon
101636.e: It is hottest at midday and in the afternoon. Sport is better early in the morning or in the evening.
101636.m: In summer, it is better to do sport in the morning or evening.

101637.q: How high can body temperature rise with heatstroke?
101637.e: Normal is about 37 degrees Celsius. With heatstroke, the temperature often rises above 40 degrees.
101637.m: A body temperature over 40 degrees is dangerous.

101638.q: How do you cool someone with heatstroke until help arrives?
101638.e: You take the person to a cool place and cool them with damp cloths. At the same time, you call the emergency number.
101638.m: When overheated, the body needs shade and cooling.

101639.e: An object blocks the light. Behind it, there is a darker area: the shadow.
101639.m: A shadow forms where something blocks the light.

101640.e: At midday, the sun is highest. The light falls steeply from above, and the shadow is short.
101640.m: Your shadow is shortest at midday.

101641.q: Your shadow is shorter than you. What does that mean?
a: The sun is strong, protect yourself
101641.e: If your shadow is shorter than you, the sun is high. Then UV radiation is strong.
101641.m: If your shadow is short, you need sun protection.

101642.q: Why is it cooler in the shade?
a: The sun does not shine directly there
101642.e: In the shade, the warm rays of the sun do not hit us directly. That is why it is more pleasant there.
101642.m: In the shade, the sun does not warm you directly.

101643.q: What is a large umbrella that gives shade called?
101643.e: A parasol keeps off the sun's rays. Underneath it is shady and cooler.

101644.q: Does shade protect you completely from UV rays?
101644.e: Some UV radiation reaches you even in the shade, for example from the sky and from bright surfaces. That is why you still need sun cream.
101644.m: Even in the shade, you need some sun protection.

a: In the morning and in the evening
101645.e: In the morning and evening, the sun is low. The light comes in at a flat angle and makes long shadows.
101645.m: A low sun makes long shadows.

101646.q: What does the abbreviation SPF on sun cream stand for?
101646.e: SPF stands for sun protection factor. It shows how strongly the cream protects against sunburn.
101646.m: The sun protection factor shows how strong the sun cream is.

101647.q: Which sun protection factor protects most strongly?
101647.e: The higher the number, the stronger the protection. SPF 50 protects more than SPF 30 or 15.
101647.m: The higher the sun protection factor, the stronger the protection.

101648.q: What must you do with sun cream after swimming?
a: Let it dry and leave it
101648.e: Water and drying yourself rub some of the cream off. That is why you put more on afterwards.
101648.m: After swimming, put on more sun cream.

101649.q: When is the best time to put on sun cream?
a: Before going out in the sun
Only once your skin is red
