103430.m: Cats purr when breathing in and out.

103431.q: Why does a kitten probably purr while drinking milk?
a: It shows its mother that all is well
It wants to frighten its mother
It wants to cool the milk
103431.e: The mother cat feels the purring and knows that her little one is fine. So purring is a way of communicating.
103431.m: Kittens talk to their mother by purring.

103432.q: Which wild cat can purr a lot like a pet cat?
103432.e: The cheetah can't roar, but it purrs. Tigers, jaguars and leopards belong to the roaring big cats.
103432.m: The cheetah purrs like a pet cat.

103433.q: What does some cats' purring sound like when they want food?
a: It has a whining sound in it
103433.e: Scientists have shown that some cats mix a high, whining sound into their purr when begging. People find this sound urgent.

103434.q: What does a tree take back from its leaves before they fall?
103434.e: Before the leaf falls, the tree pulls nutrients such as nitrogen back into its branches and trunk. In spring it uses them for new leaves.
103434.m: In autumn the tree saves nutrients for spring.

103435.q: What forms on the leaf stalk before the leaf falls in autumn?
103435.e: At the base of the leaf stalk a separation layer of cork grows. It seals the spot, and the leaf falls off with the next wind.
103435.m: A separation layer loosens the leaf from the twig.

103436.q: What colour are most leaves that have been lying on the ground for a while?
103436.e: Over time the colourful pigments break down. Brown substances are left behind, and the leaves turn brown.
103436.m: Old leaves on the ground are brown.

103437.q: In what kind of weather do autumn leaves become especially colourful?
103437.e: Sunshine and cool nights help the tree make red pigments. Then the forests glow especially beautifully.
103437.m: Sunny autumn days make the leaves colourful.

103438.q: Which young broadleaf tree often keeps its dry brown leaves until spring?
103438.e: Young beeches and oaks often keep their dry leaves on the twig all winter. Only the new buds push them off in spring.
103438.m: Young beeches often keep their brown leaves in winter.

103439.q: Why do trees in the mountains change colour earlier than in the valley?
a: Because it gets cold there sooner
Because the wind is louder there
103439.e: In the mountains it gets cool earlier in autumn. That is why the trees there start their autumn colours earlier.
103439.m: Autumn comes earlier in the mountains.

103440.q: Which vegetable contains the same orange pigment as many autumn leaves?
103440.e: The orange pigment is called carotene. It is found in carrots and also in the leaves of trees.
103440.m: Carrots and autumn leaves have the same orange pigment.

103441.q: What gives trees the signal for their autumn colours?
103441.e: Trees sense that the days are getting shorter and the nights cooler. Then they get ready for winter.
103441.m: Shorter days start autumn in the tree.

103442.q: Which tree keeps its green needles in winter?
103442.e: The spruce stays green all winter. The larch also has needles, but they turn yellow and fall off in autumn.
103442.m: The spruce stays green in winter.

103443.q: What is the smell called when rain falls on dry ground?
103443.e: The name petrichor was invented in 1964 by scientists from Australia. It describes the earthy smell after the first rain.
103443.m: The smell of rain on dry earth is called petrichor.

103444.q: Who makes the earthy-smelling substance geosmin in the soil?
103444.e: Certain soil bacteria make geosmin. When rain falls on the ground, the smell is released.
103444.m: Soil bacteria make the smell of rain.

103445.q: When does rain smell especially strong?
a: In the middle of the night
103445.e: During a dry spell, scent substances build up in the soil. The first rain releases them all at once.
103445.m: Rain smells strongest after a dry spell.

103446.q: How well can people smell the substance geosmin?
a: Only when the sun is shining
103446.e: Our noses notice geosmin even in very small amounts. That is why we smell the rain so clearly.
103446.m: Our noses are very sensitive to the smell of rain.

103447.q: How does the smell of rain get from the ground into the air?
a: The wind blows it out of the clouds
103447.e: When a drop hits the ground, tiny air bubbles rise and burst. This throws tiny scented droplets into the air.
103447.m: Raindrops fling the smell into the air.

103448.q: Which fresh, sharp smell do you sometimes notice just before a thunderstorm?
103448.e: Lightning produces the gas ozone. The wind can blow it ahead of the storm.
103448.m: Before thunderstorms it sometimes smells of ozone.

103449.q: Besides bacteria, what else adds to the smell of rain?
103449.e: During dry weather plants give off oils that collect in the soil and on stones. Rain makes them smell too.
103449.m: Plant oils also make the smell of rain.

103450.q: Which vegetable tastes earthy because it also contains geosmin?
103450.e: Beetroot naturally contains geosmin. That is why it tastes a little like soil.
103450.m: Beetroot tastes of soil because of geosmin.

103451.q: What happens to your fingers after a long bath?
103451.e: After a while in water the fingertips get lots of wrinkles. This is harmless.
103451.m: A long bath makes wrinkly fingers.

103452.q: Roughly how long in warm water does it take for your fingers to wrinkle?
103452.e: In warm water the fingertips start to wrinkle after about 5 minutes. In cold water it takes longer.
103452.m: Fingers wrinkle after just a few minutes.

103453.q: Where do you get wrinkly skin after a long bath?
103453.e: After a long bath it is mainly the fingertips and toes that get lots of wrinkles.
103453.m: Fingers wrinkle after a long bath.

103454.q: What might wrinkly fingers be useful for?
103454.e: In experiments, people with wrinkly fingers could grip wet marbles better. The wrinkles work like the tread on a tyre.
103454.m: Wrinkly fingers grip better in the wet.

103455.q: Where does skin wrinkle the most in water?
103455.e: It is mainly the fingertips and toes that get wrinkles. You hardly see anything elsewhere.
103455.m: Fingers and toes wrinkle the most.

103456.q: What happens to wrinkly fingers after a bath?
a: They stay like that for ever
They stay like that for a year
They only go smooth with cream
103456.e: After drying off, it only takes a short time for the skin to go smooth again. The wrinkles disappear on their own.
103456.m: Wrinkly fingers go smooth again by themselves.

103457.q: Are wrinkly fingers after a bath dangerous?
a: Yes, you have to see a doctor
103457.e: Wrinkly fingers after a bath are completely normal. After a short time they are smooth again.

103458.q: Do monkeys also get wrinkly fingers in water?
103458.e: Wrinkly fingers after bathing have also been seen in monkeys such as macaques.
103458.m: Some monkeys also get wrinkly fingers.

103459.q: When do we often get goosebumps?
103459.e: When we are cold, the skin reacts with goosebumps. At the same time we often start to shiver.

103460.q: What pulls the hairs up when you get goosebumps?
103460.e: There is a tiny muscle at the root of every hair. When it tightens, the hair stands up and the skin forms a little bump.
103460.m: Tiny muscles make the hairs stand up.

103461.q: How does fluffed-up fur help many animals in the cold?
103461.e: More air gets trapped between hairs that stand up. This layer of air keeps the warmth close to the body.

103462.q: Why does a cat fluff up its fur when it meets a strange dog?
103462.e: With its fur on end and its back arched, the cat looks bigger. It wants to scare the dog off.
103462.m: Fur standing on end is meant to scare enemies.

103463.q: Why do goosebumps hardly keep us humans warm?
a: We have very little body hair
103463.e: We humans don't have thick fur. That is why hardly any air gets trapped between our hairs.
103463.m: Without fur, goosebumps don't help much against the cold.

103464.q: Apart from cold, what else can give you goosebumps?
103464.e: Fear, excitement or beautiful music can also give you goosebumps. The brain then sends the same signal as when you are cold.

103465.q: Where do goosebumps get their name from?
a: They look like the skin of a plucked goose
103465.e: A goose without feathers has lots of little bumps on its skin. Our skin looks similar when we have goosebumps.
103465.m: Goosebumps are named after the plucked goose.

103467.q: Which animal raises its quills when in danger, which are actually changed hairs?
103467.e: The porcupine's quills are thick, hard hairs. When in danger, it raises them and rattles them.

103468.q: Why does chocolate melt in your mouth?
a: Because it is warm in your mouth
Because your tongue makes it cold
Because there is salt in your mouth
103468.e: Chocolate goes soft with just a little warmth. It is warm enough in your mouth, so it melts on your tongue.
103468.m: Chocolate melts in your warm mouth.

103469.e: Cocoa butter is the fat from the cocoa bean. It is solid at room temperature and melts in your mouth.

103470.q: Some chocolate was left somewhere warm and now has white patches. Can you still eat it?
a: Yes, it just doesn't look nice any more
Only if you wash it first
103470.e: The white patches form when the fat melts in the warmth and then sets again. You can still eat the chocolate.
103470.m: White patches on chocolate are usually just fat.

103472.q: Which chocolate usually goes soft faster in the warmth?
103472.e: Milk chocolate also contains milk fat. This makes it softer, so it melts more easily than dark chocolate.

103473.q: Where is the best place to keep chocolate?
103473.e: Chocolate likes it cool, but not too cold, and dry. That way it stays firm and doesn't get patches.

103474.q: What happens if a few drops of water fall into melted chocolate?
103474.e: A little water makes the sugar in the chocolate clump together. The mixture then goes stiff and crumbly.

103475.q: Which chocolate contains cocoa butter but no dark cocoa mass?
103475.e: White chocolate is made of cocoa butter, sugar and milk. Because the brown cocoa mass is missing, it is pale.
103475.m: White chocolate has no brown cocoa mass.

103476.q: Where does mineral water get its minerals from?
103476.e: The water trickles through rock for a long time. On the way it dissolves minerals such as calcium and magnesium.
103476.m: Mineral water gets its minerals from rock.

103477.q: Where do bubbles especially like to form in a glass of sparkling mineral water?
103477.e: Gas can collect on small uneven spots in the glass. The bubbles grow there and then break away.
103477.m: Bubbles form on rough spots in the glass.

103478.q: Why do the bubbles in sparkling water rise to the top?
103478.e: Gas is much lighter than water. That is why the bubbles rise and burst at the surface.
103478.m: Light gas bubbles rise to the top.

103479.q: Which Swiss region has a particularly large number of natural mineral springs?
103479.e: Around Scuol in the Lower Engadine, lots of mineral springs bubble out of the ground. You can drink from them at fountains there.
103479.m: The Lower Engadine is rich in mineral springs.

103480.q: Why do the bubbles get bigger as they rise in the glass?
a: They collect more gas on the way
103480.e: On the way up, even more gas moves out of the water into the bubble. That is why the bubbles are bigger at the top.
103480.m: Bubbles grow on their way up.

103481.q: What often happens when you open a shaken bottle of sparkling water?
103481.e: Shaking makes lots of tiny bubbles. When you open the bottle they suddenly grow and carry water out with them.

103482.q: Where does mineral water come from?
103482.e: Mineral water comes from protected underground water sources. It is bottled right at the spring.
103482.m: Mineral water comes from a spring under the ground.

103483.q: Where does the gas in naturally sparkling spring water come from?
a: From the air in the glass
103483.e: Carbon dioxide forms deep in the Earth, for example near old volcanic rock. It dissolves in the spring water.
103483.m: Natural fizz comes from deep underground.

103484.q: What is mineral water without fizz often called?
103484.e: Because nothing bubbles in it, it is called “still”. In a restaurant you can simply ask for still water.
103484.m: Water without fizz is called still water.

103485.q: How long do hiccups usually last?
103485.e: Hiccups usually stop by themselves after a few minutes.
103485.m: Hiccups usually pass after a few minutes.

a: Yes, dogs and cats for example
103487.e: Many mammals such as dogs and cats sometimes get hiccups too. Young animals get them especially often.

103488.e: Babies get hiccups very often, even before they are born. For them it is completely normal.

103489.q: What helps many people get rid of hiccups?
a: Slowly drinking a glass of water
Quickly eating a piece of bread
103489.e: Drinking slowly calms your breathing. For many people the hiccups then stop.
103489.m: Slowly drinking water often helps against hiccups.

103490.q: Can you simply switch off hiccups by willpower?
103490.e: Hiccups are a reflex, like sneezing. The body does them by itself, without us wanting to.

a: Between the chest and the belly
103491.e: The diaphragm is a large sheet of muscle under the lungs. It separates the chest from the belly.
103491.m: The diaphragm separates chest and belly.

103492.q: What does bark protect a tree from?
103492.e: Bark is the tree's protective skin. It keeps water in and fungi, insects and heat out.
103492.m: Bark is the tree's protective skin.

103493.q: What does the inner layer of the bark, the phloem, carry?
103493.e: In the phloem, sweet sap flows from the leaves to the trunk and roots. That is how the whole tree is fed.
103493.m: The phloem supplies the tree with sugar.

103494.q: What happens if you remove a ring of bark all the way round a tree?
103494.e: Without the bark the roots can no longer get any sugar. The tree slowly starves and dies.
103494.m: A tree without a ring of bark dies.

103495.q: Which forest animal likes eating tree bark in winter?
103495.e: In winter deer find little grass. So they strip bark from young trees and eat it.

103496.q: Which beetle lives under the bark and can harm spruces?
103496.e: The bark beetle bores tunnels under the bark. If there are many beetles, a weakened spruce can die.
103496.m: Bark beetles live under the bark.

103497.q: The bark of which tree was known early on as a remedy for fever and pain?
103497.e: Willow bark contains a substance that helps against pain and fever. A well-known medicine was later developed from it.

103498.q: Which spice is dried tree bark?
103498.e: Cinnamon is the dried bark of the cinnamon tree. As it dries, it rolls up into sticks.

103499.q: What happens to a small wound in the bark?
103499.e: The tree forms new tissue at the edge of the wound. Over time it grows over the damaged spot.

103500.q: What is the smallest bone in the human body called?
103500.e: The stirrup is only a few millimetres long. No other bone in the body is smaller.
103500.m: The stirrup is the smallest bone in the body.

103501.q: About how big is the stirrup bone in the ear?
103501.e: The stirrup measures only about 3 millimetres. It fits easily on a fingertip.
103501.m: The stirrup is only about 3 millimetres long.

103502.q: Which bone is one of the tiny ear bones?
103502.e: There are tiny ear bones in the middle ear. One of them is called the anvil, like the blacksmith’s tool.
103502.m: The anvil is one of the ear bones.

103503.q: What is the stirrup bone in the ear named after?
a: A foot holder used in riding
103503.e: A stirrup hangs from the saddle and holds the rider’s foot. The bone in the ear looks just like it.
103503.m: The stirrup bone is named after the foot holder on a saddle.

103504.q: What do the tiny bones in the ear help with?
103504.e: The bones pass on the vibrations from the eardrum. That is how you can hear sounds.
103504.m: The ear bones help us hear.

103505.q: What is the smallest muscle in the human body called?
103505.e: This tiny muscle is attached to a bone in the ear. It protects the ear from very loud noises.
103505.m: The smallest muscle is the stapedius.

103506.q: Where are more than half of all bones?
103506.e: Hands and feet have lots of small bones. Together they make up more than half of all bones.
103506.m: More than half of our bones are in our hands and feet.

103507.q: How many bones does a hand including the wrist have?
103507.e: The fingers, palm and wrist have 27 bones altogether. That is why the hand is so flexible.
103507.m: A hand with its wrist has 27 bones.

103508.q: About how many hairs does a person have on their head?
103508.e: About 100,000 hairs grow on the head. Fair-haired people often have a few more.
103508.m: About 100,000 hairs grow on the head.

103509.q: How many hairs from your head do you normally lose in a day?
103509.e: About 50 to 100 hairs fall out every day. That is normal, because new hairs grow back.
103509.m: You lose about 50 to 100 hairs every day.

103510.q: What is hair mainly made of?
103510.e: Hair is mainly made of keratin, a horny substance. Nails are made of the same material.
103510.m: Hair is made of keratin, a horny substance.

103511.q: Why does hair go grey in old age?
103511.e: In old age the hair root makes less pigment. Without pigment, hair looks grey or white.
103511.m: Grey hair has too little pigment.

103512.q: Does a child’s heart beat faster or slower than an adult’s?
103512.e: Children have a smaller heart. That is why it has to beat more often than an adult’s heart.

103513.q: About how long are all the blood vessels of an adult put together?
103513.e: If you laid all the blood vessels end to end, they would be about 100,000 kilometres long. Most of them are tiny and thin.
103513.m: All blood vessels together are about 100,000 kilometres long.

103514.q: About how many times would all of a person’s blood vessels go round the Earth?
a: About two and a half times
Only a tenth of the way
103514.e: The Earth’s circumference at the equator is about 40,000 kilometres. So about 100,000 kilometres of blood vessels would go round about two and a half times.
103514.m: A person’s blood vessels would go round the Earth about two and a half times.

103516.q: About how heavy is an adult’s skin?
103516.e: An adult’s skin weighs several kilograms. Depending on whether you count the layer under the skin, it is about 3 to 10 kilograms.

103517.q: About how large is the area of an adult’s skin?
103517.e: If you spread the skin out, it would be about 1.5 to 2 square metres. That is as much as a big bath towel.
103517.m: An adult’s skin is about 2 square metres.

a: On the sole of the foot
103518.e: The skin on the sole of the foot is especially thick. It has to put up with a lot when you walk.
103518.m: The skin is thickest on the sole of the foot.

103519.e: The skin on the eyelid is very thin. That way you can open and close your eye easily.
103519.m: The skin is thinnest on the eyelid.

103520.q: About how often does the top layer of skin renew itself?
103520.e: Old skin flakes fall off all the time. In about four weeks the top layer is new.
103520.m: The top layer of skin renews itself about every month.

103521.q: Do your eyes move while you sleep?
103521.e: In dream sleep, the eyes move quickly back and forth under the lids. That is why this phase is called REM sleep.
103521.m: When you dream, your eyes move quickly.

103522.q: About how big is an adult’s eyeball?
103522.e: An eyeball is about 2.5 centimetres across. That is about the size of a marble or a bit bigger.
103522.m: An eyeball is about 2.5 centimetres across.

103523.q: What do your eyes do when you look to the left?
a: Both turn at the same time
103523.e: The eye muscles of both eyes work together. That way both eyes look at the same point.
103523.m: Both eyes move at the same time.

103524.q: About how long does a blink last?
103524.e: A blink is very quick. It only lasts a fraction of a second.
103524.m: A blink lasts less than half a second.

103526.q: What do you almost always do automatically when you sneeze?
103526.e: When you sneeze, your eyes close all by themselves. That is a reflex.
103526.m: When you sneeze, your eyes close by themselves.

103527.q: Can bright sunlight make some people sneeze?
103527.e: Some people have to sneeze when they suddenly look into bright light. This is called photic sneezing.
103527.m: Bright light can make some people sneeze.

103528.q: How far can droplets fly when you sneeze?
103528.e: Fine droplets can float several metres when you sneeze. That is why you should keep your distance and turn away when sneezing.
103528.m: Sneeze droplets can fly several metres.

103529.q: What is the tongue made of?
103529.e: The tongue is made of several muscles that work together. That is why it can move so well.
103529.m: The tongue is made of several muscles.

103530.q: Is the tongue the strongest muscle in the body?
a: Yes, but only in the morning
103530.e: The tongue is very flexible and works hard. But it is not the strongest muscle.
103530.m: The tongue is not the strongest muscle.

103531.q: Which taste is one of the basic tastes?
103531.e: The tongue can tell sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami apart. Dark chocolate, for example, tastes bitter.

103532.q: About how many taste buds does a person have?
103532.e: A person has about 2,000 to 5,000 taste buds, most of them on the tongue. We taste with them.
103532.m: A person has a few thousand taste buds.

103533.q: Who was the tallest person whose height was reliably measured?
103533.e: Robert Wadlow died in 1940. According to Guinness World Records he is the tallest person ever measured.
103533.m: Robert Wadlow was the tallest person ever measured.

103534.q: How tall was Robert Wadlow, the tallest person ever measured?
103534.e: Robert Wadlow grew to 2.72 metres. He needed huge, specially made shoes.

103535.q: Which country is Sultan Kösen, the tallest living man (as of 2025), from?
103535.e: Sultan Kösen comes from Turkey. According to Guinness World Records he is the tallest living man.
103535.m: Sultan Kösen from Turkey is the tallest living man.

103536.q: Why are you a little shorter in the evening than in the morning?
a: The discs in your spine get squashed
103536.e: Soft discs lie between the vertebrae. When you stand and walk, they get squashed together.
103536.m: The discs in your spine get squashed during the day.

103537.q: When does a person grow fastest?
a: In the first year of life
103537.e: In its first year a baby grows about 25 centimetres. You never grow that fast again.
103537.m: You grow fastest in your first year of life.

103538.q: About how tall was Chandra Bahadur Dangi, the shortest adult man ever measured?
103538.e: Chandra Bahadur Dangi from Nepal was 54.6 centimetres tall. He died in 2015.
103538.m: The shortest man ever measured was only about 55 centimetres tall.

103539.q: About how tall is Rumeysa Gelgi, the tallest living woman (as of 2025)?
103539.e: Rumeysa Gelgi was measured at 2.15 metres. According to Guinness World Records she is the tallest living woman.
103539.m: The tallest living woman is about 2.15 metres tall.

103540.q: About how much of an adult’s body is water?
103540.e: An adult’s body is about 60 per cent water. That is more than half.
103540.m: An adult is about 60 per cent water.

103541.q: Does a baby have more or less water in its body than an adult?
103541.e: A newborn baby is about 75 per cent water. The share goes down with age.
103541.m: Babies have more water in their bodies than adults.

103542.q: Which drink is a good and cheap thirst quencher in Switzerland?
103542.e: Tap water in Switzerland is clean and perfectly safe to drink. It has no sugar.
103542.m: Tap water is a good thirst quencher.

103543.q: Do you also lose water when you breathe out?
103543.e: Your breath contains water vapour. You can see it when you breathe on a cold window.
103543.m: When you breathe out, you lose water as water vapour.

103544.q: What does fresh sweat smell like?
103544.e: Fresh sweat is mostly water and a little salt and hardly smells. The smell only develops later on the skin.
103544.m: Fresh sweat smells of almost nothing.

103545.q: Where do you have especially many sweat glands?
a: On the palms and soles of the feet
103545.e: There are especially many sweat glands on the palms and soles. That is why they quickly get damp when you are excited.
103545.m: Palms and soles have especially many sweat glands.

103546.q: How many stirrup bones does a person have?
103546.e: There is a stirrup bone in each ear. Because we have two ears, there are two.
103546.m: Everyone has two stirrup bones, one in each ear.

103547.q: Which thin membrane in the ear is the hammer bone attached to?
103547.e: The hammer is connected to the eardrum. When the eardrum vibrates, the hammer moves too.
103547.m: The hammer is attached to the eardrum.

103548.q: About how much does the stirrup bone in the ear weigh?
103548.e: The stirrup weighs only a few milligrams. It is much lighter than a grain of rice.
103548.m: The stirrup weighs only a few milligrams.

103549.q: How many ear bones does a person have in both ears together?
103549.e: There are three ear bones in each ear. With two ears that is 3 times 2, so 6.
103549.m: Together, both ears have six ear bones.

103550.q: Which substance in the body is even harder than bone?
103550.e: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the whole body. It is even harder than any bone.
103550.m: Tooth enamel is harder than bone.

103551.e: Bones are made of living cells and are supplied with blood. That is why they can grow and heal.
103551.m: Bones are alive and can heal.

103552.q: Which is the longest bone in the arm?
103552.e: The humerus reaches from the shoulder to the elbow. It is the longest bone in the arm.
103552.m: The humerus is the longest bone in the arm.

103553.q: Why does a baby have soft spots on its head?
a: The skull bones have not grown together yet
The baby has no hair yet
The head is full of water
103553.e: In babies, the bones of the head have not fully grown together yet. In between there are soft spots that later become hard.
103553.m: Babies have soft spots on their heads because the bones are still growing.

103554.q: About how long does a hair on your head grow before it falls out?
103554.e: A hair on your head usually grows for several years. Then it falls out and a new one grows.
103554.m: A hair on your head grows for several years.

103555.q: About how thick is a single hair on your head?
103555.e: A hair is only about 0.05 to 0.1 millimetres thick. That is why you only see it well when it is longer.
103555.m: A hair is less than a millimetre thick.

103556.q: Does hair grow faster if you cut it often?
103556.e: Hair grows from the root under the skin. Whether you cut the ends makes no difference.
103556.m: Cutting your hair doesn’t make it grow faster.

103557.q: About how many hairs does a person have on their whole body?
103557.e: Fine little hairs grow almost everywhere on the body. Together there are several million.
103557.m: A person has several million hairs on the whole body.

103558.q: Why doesn’t having your hair cut hurt?
a: There are no nerves in hair
103558.e: There are no nerves in the hair itself. You only feel something at the root in the skin, which is why pulling hair hurts.

103559.q: A heart beats 70 times a minute. How many times does it beat in 10 minutes?
103559.e: You calculate 70 times 10. That makes 700 beats.
103559.m: At 70 beats a minute, a heart beats 700 times in 10 minutes.

103560.q: Since when does a person’s heart beat?
103560.e: The heart starts beating very early in the mother’s tummy. So it beats long before birth.
103560.m: The heart beats even before birth.

103561.q: About how much blood does the heart pump in one minute at rest?
103561.e: At rest, an adult’s heart pumps about 5 litres of blood a minute. During sport it is much more.
103561.m: At rest the heart pumps about 5 litres of blood a minute.

103562.q: About how much blood does the heart pump in a single day?
103562.e: A day has 1,440 minutes. At about 5 litres a minute, that is over 7,000 litres.
103562.m: The heart pumps over 7,000 litres of blood every day.

103563.q: About how many times does an adult’s heart beat in a year?
103563.e: The heart beats about 100,000 times a day. Times 365 days, that makes over 30 million beats.
103563.m: The heart beats over 30 million times a year.

103564.q: About how long does a heartbeat last at rest?
103564.e: At rest the heart beats about 60 to 80 times a minute. So one beat lasts about one second.
103564.m: A heartbeat at rest lasts about one second.

103565.q: About how long does blood take for one full round of the body?
103565.e: Blood flows from the heart through the body and back again. At rest, one round takes about one minute.
103565.m: Blood flows once round the body in about one minute.

103566.q: Why do you bleed even from a small scratch?
a: There are fine blood vessels everywhere in the skin
The skin is filled with blood like a balloon
The heart is right under the skin
Scratches always hit a big vein
103566.e: Fine blood vessels reach almost to the surface of the skin. That is why even a small scratch bleeds.
103566.m: Fine blood vessels lie everywhere just under the skin.

103567.q: About how much blood does a child weighing 30 kilograms have?
103567.e: A person has about 70 to 80 millilitres of blood per kilogram of body weight. At 30 kilograms that is about 2 litres.
103567.m: A child weighing 30 kilograms has about 2 litres of blood.

103568.q: About how many red blood cells does an adult have?
103568.e: About 25 trillion red blood cells float in an adult’s blood. That is a number with 14 digits.
103568.m: An adult has several trillion red blood cells.

103569.q: About how much of your body weight is blood?
103569.e: Blood makes up about 7 to 8 per cent of body weight. At 70 kilograms that is about 5 kilograms.
103569.m: Blood makes up about 7 to 8 per cent of body weight.

103570.q: What is the top layer of the skin called?
103570.e: The skin has several layers. The outermost one is the epidermis.
103570.m: The top layer of the skin is called the epidermis.

103571.q: What is the skin layer directly under the epidermis called?
103571.e: Under the epidermis lies the dermis. It is firm and elastic and contains blood vessels and nerves.
103571.m: The dermis lies under the epidermis.

103572.q: About how many tiny flakes of skin do you lose every minute?
103572.e: The skin constantly sheds old cells. Every minute it is many thousands of tiny flakes.
103572.m: We lose thousands of skin flakes every minute.

103573.q: Which muscles are among the fastest in the body?
103573.e: The muscles that move the eye work lightning fast. They are among the fastest muscles in the body.
103573.m: The eye muscles are among the fastest muscles.

103574.q: How do your eyes move when you read a line?
103574.e: When you read, your eyes jump from word to word. In between they stop very briefly.
103574.m: When reading, the eyes move in small jumps.

103575.q: Can a person turn their eyes independently in different directions like a chameleon?
a: Yes, but only in their sleep
103575.e: In humans, the muscles of both eyes work closely together. A chameleon, on the other hand, can move each eye separately.
103575.m: People can’t turn their eyes separately in different directions.

103576.q: What helps your eyes recover after reading for a long time?
a: Looking very closely at the page
103576.e: When you look into the distance, your eyes have to work less. That way they can relax after reading for a long time.
103576.m: Looking into the distance relaxes the eyes.

103577.q: What moves your eyes up, down and to the side?
103577.e: There are small muscles on each eye. They turn the eye in all directions.

103578.q: What do you do just before you sneeze?
103578.e: Before sneezing you take a deep breath. Then the air is pushed out through the nose and mouth with great force.
103578.m: Before sneezing you breathe in deeply.

103579.q: What do people often say in French when someone sneezes?
103579.e: In French-speaking Switzerland and in France, people often say “À tes souhaits!” after a sneeze. It means roughly “To your wishes!”.
103579.m: In French, people often say “À tes souhaits!” after a sneeze.

a: Yes, for example dogs and cats
103580.e: Many animals with a nose can sneeze. Dogs and cats sneeze, for example, when their nose is irritated.
103580.m: Dogs and cats can sneeze too.

103581.q: Which spice makes many people sneeze when it gets into their nose?
103581.e: Ground pepper strongly irritates the nose. That is why you often have to sneeze when you smell it.
103581.m: Pepper in the nose makes many people sneeze.

103582.q: What colour is a healthy tongue usually?
103582.e: A healthy tongue is usually pink and moist. A thin pale coating is normal.
103582.m: A healthy tongue is usually pink.

103583.q: Can everyone roll their tongue into a tube?
103583.e: Some people can roll up the edges of their tongue, others can’t. That is completely normal.
103583.m: Not everyone can roll their tongue.

103584.q: How fast does a small injury on the tongue usually heal?
103584.e: The tongue has a very good blood supply and is always moist. That is why small bite wounds usually heal within a few days.
103584.m: Small wounds on the tongue heal very fast.

103585.q: About how long is an adult’s tongue?
103585.e: From the throat to the tip, an adult’s tongue measures about 10 centimetres. A large part of it is hidden at the back of the mouth.
103585.m: An adult’s tongue is about 10 centimetres long.

103586.q: In which country did Robert Wadlow, the tallest person ever measured, live?
103586.e: Robert Wadlow was born in 1918 in the state of Illinois in the USA. He lived there all his life.
103586.m: Robert Wadlow lived in the USA.

103587.q: About how tall is Sultan Kösen, the tallest living man (as of 2025)?
103587.e: Sultan Kösen was measured at 2.51 metres. That makes him taller than almost any door.
103587.m: The tallest living man is about 2.51 metres tall.

103588.q: Which vegetable is almost entirely water?
103588.e: A cucumber is about 95 per cent water. That is why it is so refreshing in summer.
103588.m: A cucumber is almost entirely water.

103589.q: About how much of the brain is water?
103589.e: The brain is about three quarters water. That is why drinking is important for thinking too.
103589.m: The brain is about three quarters water.

103590.q: Does the body also get water from food?
103590.e: Fruit, vegetables and soups contain lots of water. So you also take in water when you eat.
103590.m: The body also takes in water with food.

103591.q: What is often left on a sweaty T-shirt after it dries?
103591.e: The water in sweat evaporates and the salt stays behind. That makes white marks on the fabric.
103591.m: Dried sweat leaves white salt marks.

103592.q: How much sweat can a person lose in an hour doing sport in great heat?
103592.e: In heat and with effort, the sweat glands work at full speed. Then you can lose more than a litre in an hour.
103592.m: Doing sport in the heat, you can lose over a litre of sweat an hour.

103593.q: Do you sweat in your sleep too?
103593.e: Even during sleep, the sweat glands release a little sweat. Under a thick duvet often even more.
103593.m: You sweat a little in your sleep too.

103594.q: Which animal has hardly any sweat glands and cools off in mud?
103594.e: Pigs can hardly sweat. That is why they like to wallow in cool mud.
103594.m: Pigs cool off in mud because they hardly sweat.

103595.q: Who usually starts sweating earlier during sport?
103595.e: The bodies of trained athletes learn to cool down faster. That is why they often sweat earlier.
103595.m: Trained athletes usually start sweating earlier.

103596.q: About how much does a person sweat on a normal day without sport?
103596.e: Even without sport, the skin constantly releases a little sweat. On a normal day that is about half a litre.
103596.m: Without sport you sweat about half a litre a day.

103597.q: A child’s heart beats 90 times a minute. How many times does it beat in 2 minutes?
103597.e: You calculate 90 times 2. That makes 180 beats.
103597.m: At 90 beats a minute, a heart beats 180 times in two minutes.

103598.q: You drink 6 glasses of 2 decilitres of water each. How many decilitres is that altogether?
103598.e: You calculate 6 times 2 decilitres. That is 12 decilitres.
103598.m: Six glasses of 2 decilitres each make 12 decilitres.

103599.q: A child loses 1 litre of sweat. How many glasses of 2 decilitres each must they drink to replace it?
103599.e: 1 litre is 10 decilitres. 10 decilitres divided by 2 decilitres makes 5 glasses.
103599.m: For one litre you need five glasses of 2 decilitres each.

103600.q: Which is bigger: the Sun or the Earth?
103600.e: The Sun is huge. A great many Earths would fit inside it.
103600.m: The Sun is much bigger than the Earth.

103602.q: How long has the Sun been around?
a: Since the time of the knights
103602.e: The Sun is ancient. It was there long before there were people or dinosaurs.
103602.m: The Sun has been around for a very, very long time.

103604.q: How much of the total mass of our solar system is in the Sun?
103604.e: The Sun is so heavy that it makes up over 99 percent of the mass of the solar system. All the planets together are much lighter.
103604.m: The Sun contains over 99 percent of the mass of the solar system.

103605.q: Roughly how long does the Moon take to go once round the Earth?
103605.e: The Moon circles the Earth in just over 27 days. That is about 4 weeks.
103605.m: The Moon takes about 4 weeks to go once round the Earth.

103607.q: Is the Moon bigger or smaller than the Earth?
103607.e: The Moon is much smaller than the Earth. It only looks big because it is close to us.
103607.m: The Moon is smaller than the Earth.

103608.q: What are the large dark areas on the Moon called?
103608.e: People used to think the dark areas were seas. Today we know they are plains of dark rock, but the name stuck.
103608.m: The dark areas on the Moon are called lunar seas.

103609.q: Why do footprints on the Moon last a very long time?
a: There is no wind or rain there
The ground is made of concrete
103609.e: On the Moon there is no wind and no rain. That is why nothing wipes away the astronauts' footprints.
103609.m: Without wind and rain, footprints on the Moon last a long time.

103610.q: What is the temperature like on the Moon?
a: Very hot by day, very cold at night
103610.e: The Moon has no layer of air to keep in the warmth. That is why it gets over 100 degrees by day and very cold at night.
103610.m: On the Moon it is very hot by day and very cold at night.

103611.q: What did people use to fly to the Moon?
103611.e: Only a rocket is strong enough to fly into space and to the Moon. Aeroplanes and balloons need air and stay close to the Earth.
103611.m: You fly to the Moon in a rocket.

103612.q: Why doesn't the Moon look the same every night?
a: We see different parts of its lit side
The Moon gets eaten a bit smaller every day
103612.e: The Sun always lights up one half of the Moon. Because the Moon circles the Earth, we see a different part of that half each day.
103612.m: Each day we see a different part of the Moon's lit side.

103613.q: The crescent Moon is lit on the right and looks like a bracket “)”. What is the Moon doing?
103613.e: Where we live, the waxing Moon is lit on the right. The waning Moon, on the other hand, is lit on the left.
103613.m: If the crescent is lit on the right, the Moon is waxing.

103614.q: What do you call the Moon when exactly half of it is lit?
103614.e: When we see exactly half of the Moon's disc bright, we call it a half moon. This happens twice a month.
103614.m: When half is lit, it is called a half moon.

103615.q: What is the thin, curved shape of the Moon called?
103615.e: Shortly after and shortly before the new moon you only see a thin strip. It is curved like a sickle.
103615.m: The thin shape of the Moon is called a crescent.

103616.q: Roughly how many full moons are there in a year?
103616.e: A lunar cycle lasts just under a month. That is why there are 12 and sometimes 13 full moons in a year.
103616.m: There are 12 or 13 full moons in a year.

103618.q: Can you see the Moon during the day too?
103618.e: The Moon is often in the sky during the day too. Then it looks pale against the bright sky.
103618.m: You can often see the Moon during the day too.

103619.q: How long does the Earth take to turn once on its own axis?
103619.e: The Earth turns once on its own axis in about 24 hours. That is one day.
103619.m: The Earth turns once on its axis in about 24 hours.

103620.q: What is the imaginary line the Earth turns around called?
103620.e: The Earth's axis goes through the North Pole and the South Pole. The Earth turns around this imaginary line.
103620.m: The Earth turns around its axis.

103621.q: Roughly how fast does the ground at the equator move because of the Earth's turning?
103621.e: The distance round the Earth at the equator is about 40,000 kilometres. This distance is covered in 24 hours, which is about 1670 km/h.
103621.m: At the equator the ground moves at over 1600 km/h.

103622.q: Where on Earth do you move most slowly because of the Earth's turning?
103622.e: At the poles you almost just turn on the spot. At the equator, on the other hand, you cover the greatest distance.
103622.m: At the poles you move most slowly because of the Earth's turning.

103623.q: Where does the Sun rise earlier in the morning: in Japan or in Switzerland?
a: In both countries at the same time
In a different country every day
103623.e: The Earth turns from west to east. Japan is far to the east of Switzerland, so morning comes earlier there.
103623.m: The Sun rises earlier in Japan than in Switzerland.

103624.q: When it is midday where we are, is it midday all over the world?
a: Yes, everywhere at the same time
No, because the Moon moves the time
103624.e: The Earth turns. That is why the Sun is not at its highest everywhere at the same time. When it is midday here, it is morning or night somewhere else.
103624.m: Because the Earth turns, it is not midday everywhere at once.

103625.q: The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours. How many degrees does it turn in one hour?
103625.e: You work out 360 degrees divided by 24 hours. That makes 15 degrees per hour.
103625.m: The Earth turns 15 degrees in one hour.

103626.q: Which planet orbits closest to the Sun?
103626.e: Mercury is the innermost planet. It goes round the Sun in only about 88 days.
103626.m: Mercury orbits closest to the Sun.

103627.q: Which planet is called “the Red Planet”?
103627.e: The ground on Mars contains lots of rusty iron. That is why it glows reddish.
103627.m: Mars is called the Red Planet.

103628.e: Since 2006 Pluto has no longer counted as a planet. It is now seen as a dwarf planet.
103628.m: Pluto is a dwarf planet today.

103630.q: Which well-known group of seven stars looks like a cart with a long handle?
103630.e: Seven bright stars form the Plough, which in German is called the Big Cart. It is part of the constellation of the Great Bear.
103630.m: The Plough looks like a cart with a long handle.

103631.q: What is the star that stands almost exactly in the north of the sky called?
103631.e: The Pole Star is almost exactly above the Earth's North Pole. That is why it shows the direction north.

103632.q: What is the bright band of many stars that you see in the sky on dark nights called?
103632.e: On really dark nights you can see a bright strip in the sky. It is made of countless stars and is called the Milky Way.
103632.m: The bright band of stars in the sky is called the Milky Way.

103633.q: What colour are the hottest stars?
103633.e: The colour of a star gives away its temperature. Red stars are cooler, blue stars are the hottest.

103634.q: What does a rocket push out of the back so that it flies forwards?
103634.e: The engine pushes hot gases out of the back with great force. That pushes the rocket forwards.
103634.m: A rocket flies because it pushes hot gases out of the back.

103635.q: What do people count before a rocket launch?
103635.e: Before the launch the last seconds are counted backwards. This is called a countdown.
103635.m: Before a rocket launch you count backwards to zero.

103636.q: Roughly how fast does a rocket have to fly so that it can circle the Earth?
103636.e: To avoid falling back to Earth, you need about 7.8 kilometres per second. That is around 28,000 km/h.

103637.q: Why do big rockets have several stages?
a: Empty parts are dropped so it gets lighter
103637.e: When the fuel of a stage is used up, the stage is dropped. The rocket gets lighter and can go faster.
103637.m: Rockets drop empty stages to get lighter.

103638.q: What does a rocket have to take with it because there is no air in space?
103638.e: Fuel needs oxygen to burn. Because there is no air in space, the rocket takes it along itself.
103638.m: A rocket takes its own oxygen along.

103639.q: Who was the first person to fly into space in a rocket, in 1961?
103639.e: Yuri Gagarin from the Soviet Union circled the Earth on 12 April 1961. He was the first person in space.
103639.m: Yuri Gagarin was the first person in space in 1961.

103640.q: What pushes a water rocket made from a plastic bottle up into the air?
a: Water forced out by air pressure
103640.e: You pump air into the bottle with some water in it. The air forces the water out at the bottom, and the bottle shoots upwards.
103640.m: A water rocket flies because air pressure forces the water out.

103641.q: What was the name of the dog that circled the Earth in a rocket in 1957, one of the first animals to do so?
103641.e: The dog Laika flew into space in 1957 on the satellite Sputnik 2. She was the first animal in orbit round the Earth.
103641.m: The dog Laika circled the Earth in 1957.

a: An object that circles a planet
103642.e: A satellite circles a bigger body in space. There are natural ones like the Moon and artificial ones that people have built.

103643.q: What are weather satellites needed for?
a: To watch clouds and weather from above
103643.e: Weather satellites photograph the Earth from above. That way you can see where clouds and storms are moving.
103643.m: Weather satellites watch the weather from above.

103644.q: How does a satnav in a car know where it is?
103644.e: Navigation satellites such as GPS send out signals all the time. The device works out its position from them.
103644.m: A satnav finds its position with the help of satellites.

103645.q: Can you see some satellites at night without a telescope?
a: Yes, as moving points of light
103645.e: Satellites reflect sunlight. Some, like the ISS space station, can be seen as bright points moving across the sky.
103645.m: Some satellites can be seen at night as moving points of light.

103646.q: Why doesn't a satellite simply fall down to Earth?
a: It flies round the Earth very fast
It is fixed with a rope
It has wings like a bird
103646.e: A satellite is actually falling towards the Earth all the time. But because it moves sideways so fast, it keeps falling round the Earth.
103646.m: A satellite doesn't fall down because it flies round the Earth very fast.

a: Old satellites and parts in space
103647.e: Old satellites, rocket parts and fragments keep circling the Earth. They can be dangerous for new satellites.
103647.m: Space junk is old satellites and parts circling the Earth.

103648.q: What does the navigation app on a mobile phone use satellites for?
a: To work out its own position
103648.e: Satellites such as the GPS ones send out signals all the time. From how long several signals take to arrive, the phone works out where it is.
103648.m: Navigation satellites help to work out your position.

103649.q: What is a shooting star really?
a: A small piece of rock burning up in the air
103649.e: Small particles from space race into the Earth's atmosphere. As they do, they glow and burn up.
103649.m: A shooting star is a small piece of rock burning up.

103650.q: What do you call a rock from space that reaches the ground?
103650.e: Bigger chunks don't burn up completely. The part that lands on the ground is called a meteorite.
103650.m: A rock from space on the ground is called a meteorite.

103651.q: What is the meteor shower that you can see well every year in August called?
103651.e: In mid-August you can see especially many shooting stars. They seem to come from the constellation Perseus and are therefore called the Perseids.
103651.m: In August you can see the Perseids.

103652.q: Why does a shooting star glow?
a: It gets very hot in the air
103652.e: The particle races into the air at high speed. It gets so hot that it glows.
103652.m: A shooting star glows because it gets very hot in the air.

103653.q: How fast does a shooting star fly?
103653.e: Shooting stars race into the atmosphere much faster than any aeroplane. That is why you only see them flash for a moment.
103653.m: Shooting stars are much faster than an aeroplane.

103654.q: Where do most shooting stars burn up?
a: High up in the air, higher than aeroplanes
103654.e: Most shooting stars light up high in the atmosphere. That is much higher than aeroplanes fly.
103654.m: Shooting stars burn up high in the air.

103655.q: In which month can you see especially many shooting stars where we live?
103655.e: Every year in August the Earth passes through a cloud of dust left behind by a comet. Then you can see lots of shooting stars on clear nights.
103655.m: There are especially many shooting stars in August.

103656.q: What can you use to look at a solar eclipse safely?
103656.e: Even a partly covered Sun can badly damage your eyes. Only special eclipse glasses filter out enough light.
103656.m: Only look at a solar eclipse with eclipse glasses.

103657.q: During a total solar eclipse, what can you see around the covered Sun?
103657.e: When the Moon covers the Sun completely, you can see its outer layer. It shines like a ring of rays and is called the corona.
103657.m: During a total solar eclipse you can see a ring of rays.

103658.q: At most, how long does the complete darkness last during a total solar eclipse?
103658.e: The Moon's shadow moves quickly across the Earth. That is why the complete darkness in one place lasts about 7.5 minutes at most.
103658.m: A total solar eclipse lasts only a few minutes.

103659.q: In which country could the total solar eclipse of 12 August 2026 be seen?
103659.e: The Moon's full shadow passed over Greenland, Iceland and Spain. In Switzerland the Sun was only partly covered.
103659.m: The total solar eclipse of 2026 could be seen in Spain.

103660.q: What happens to the temperature during a total solar eclipse?
103660.e: During the eclipse hardly any sunlight arrives. That is why the air cools down noticeably.
103660.m: It gets cooler during a total solar eclipse.

103661.q: How do many birds behave during a total solar eclipse?
a: They go quiet as in the evening
103661.e: Many animals think the sudden darkness is evening. Birds often stop singing.
103661.m: Many birds go quiet during a total solar eclipse.

103662.q: During a solar eclipse the Moon sometimes covers only part of the Sun. What does the Sun look like then?
a: As if someone had bitten a piece off
103662.e: If the Moon only moves partly in front of the Sun, a round piece is missing from it. This is called a partial solar eclipse.
103662.m: In a partial solar eclipse a piece of the Sun is missing.

103663.q: Can a total solar eclipse be seen everywhere on Earth at the same time?
a: No, only in a narrow strip
103663.e: The Moon's full shadow is only a small patch on the Earth. It moves across the Earth as a narrow strip.
103663.m: A total solar eclipse can only be seen in a narrow strip.

103664.q: Why are there seasons on Earth?
a: The Earth is closer to the Sun in summer
The Sun sometimes shines more strongly, sometimes more weakly
The Moon covers the Sun in winter
103664.e: Because the Earth's axis is tilted, each half of the Earth gets sometimes more and sometimes less sunlight during the year. That is how summer and winter come about.
103664.m: Seasons happen because the Earth's axis is tilted.

103665.q: Around which date does spring begin where we live?
103665.e: Around 20 March day and night are about the same length. Then spring begins where we live.

103666.q: In which month does astronomical autumn begin where we live?
103666.e: Around 22 or 23 September day and night are the same length again. Then astronomical autumn begins where we live.

103667.q: Which season is it in Australia when it is summer where we live?
103667.e: Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere. There the seasons are exactly the other way round from ours.
103667.m: When it is summer here, it is winter in Australia.

103668.q: Which seasons do many countries near the equator have instead of summer and winter?
103668.e: At the equator the Sun is high all year round, so it is always warm. Instead of summer and winter, a rainy season and a dry season often take turns there.
103668.m: At the equator there is often a rainy season and a dry season instead of summer and winter.

103669.q: How many days does a leap year have?
103669.e: The Earth needs a little more than 365 days to go once round the Sun. That is why there is a 29 February almost every 4 years.

103670.q: Is the Earth closest to the Sun in summer?
a: No, it is closest at the beginning of January
103670.e: The Earth's orbit is almost a circle. The Earth is closest to the Sun at the beginning of January, in the middle of our winter.
103670.m: The Earth is closest to the Sun at the beginning of January.

103671.q: Which large space telescope was launched into space on 25 December 2021?
103671.e: The James Webb Space Telescope was launched at Christmas 2021. It observes very distant galaxies with infrared light.
103671.m: The James Webb Space Telescope was launched in 2021.

103672.q: Which famous space telescope has been circling the Earth since 1990?
103672.e: The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990. It has taken many famous pictures of stars and galaxies.
103672.m: The Hubble telescope has been circling the Earth since 1990.

103673.q: Why are large telescopes often built on high mountains?
a: Air and clouds get in the way less there
103673.e: On high mountains there is less air above the telescope. You are also often above the clouds and far away from city lights.
103673.m: On high mountains air and clouds get in the telescope's way less.

103674.q: What does a telescope collect so that you can see distant stars?
103674.e: With a lens or a mirror, a telescope collects much more light than the eye. That way you can see very faint stars too.

103675.q: What does a reflecting telescope use instead of a large lens?
103675.e: A reflecting telescope collects the light with a curved mirror. Even the biggest telescopes in the world are reflecting telescopes.
103675.m: A reflecting telescope collects light with a curved mirror.

103676.q: Why must you never look at the Sun through a telescope?
103676.e: A telescope concentrates the sunlight very strongly. That can destroy your eye in an instant.
103676.m: Never look at the Sun through a telescope.

103677.q: What is the well-known public observatory in the middle of Zurich called?
103677.e: The Urania Observatory has stood in the middle of Zurich since 1907. There you can look at the sky through a large telescope.
103677.m: The Urania Observatory is in Zurich.

103678.q: What is the part of a telescope you look into called?
103678.e: The eyepiece is at the end where your eye goes. You look at the image through this small piece of lens.
103678.m: You look into a telescope through the eyepiece.

103679.q: What is the main job of the cell wall of a plant cell?
103679.e: The cell wall is a sturdy covering around the cell. It supports the cell and gives it a firm shape.
103679.m: The cell wall makes the plant cell sturdy.

103680.q: What does the cell wall prevent when a plant cell takes in a lot of water?
103680.e: When the cell takes in water, its contents push outwards. The firm cell wall pushes back, so the plant cell doesn't burst.
103680.m: The cell wall protects the plant cell from bursting.

103682.q: Which substance from plant cell walls is used as a gelling agent when making jam?
103682.e: Pectin is a component of cell walls and is found in especially large amounts in apples and citrus fruits. It makes jam set; gelatine, on the other hand, comes from animals.
103682.m: Pectin from plant cell walls makes jam set.

103683.q: Which living things have cell walls made of chitin instead of cellulose?
103683.e: Fungi are not plants. Their cell walls are made of chitin, the same substance that is found in the shells of insects.
103683.m: Fungi have cell walls made of chitin.

103684.q: Do animal cells have a cell wall?
103684.e: Animal cells are surrounded only by a thin, flexible cell membrane. They have no firm cell wall.
103684.m: Animal cells have no cell wall.

103685.q: Does the cell wall let water and dissolved substances through?
103685.e: The cell wall is like a coarse net of fibres and lets water and small dissolved substances through easily. The real selection is only made by the cell membrane.
103685.m: The cell wall is highly permeable to water.

103686.q: In which plant material do the cells have especially thick, lignified cell walls?
a: In the wood of a tree trunk
In the petal of a rose
In the flesh of a tomato
103686.e: In wood, the cell walls are greatly thickened and lignified. That is why a tree trunk is so hard and strong.
103686.m: Wood is hard because its cell walls are thick and lignified.

103687.q: Which property best describes the cell membrane?
a: It only lets certain substances through
It lets no substances through at all
It lets all substances through equally
103687.e: The cell membrane is partially permeable (selectively permeable). It controls which substances get into and out of the cell.
103687.m: The cell membrane selects which substances get into the cell.

103688.q: Where is the cell membrane in a plant cell?
a: On the inside, close against the cell wall
On the outside of the cell wall
In the middle of the nucleus
103688.e: The cell membrane encloses the cytoplasm and, in plant cells, lies close against the inside of the cell wall.
103688.m: In plants, the cell membrane lies against the inside of the cell wall.

103689.q: What is the cell membrane mainly made of?
a: A double layer of fatty substances
103689.e: The cell membrane is a very thin double layer of lipids, which are fatty substances. It surrounds the whole cell.
103689.m: The cell membrane is a double layer of fatty substances with proteins built in.

103690.q: What is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane called?
103690.e: In osmosis, water moves through a partially permeable membrane towards the side with the higher concentration of dissolved substances.
103690.m: Osmosis is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane.

103691.q: What happens to a lettuce leaf that lies in strong salt water for a long time?
a: It goes limp because it loses water
103691.e: The salt draws water out of the cells. The cells shrink and the leaf goes soft and limp.
103691.m: Salt water draws water out of plant cells.

103692.q: Which cell part do plant cells, animal cells and bacteria have in common?
103692.e: Every living cell is surrounded by a cell membrane. A cellulose wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole, on the other hand, are only found in plants.
103692.m: All living cells have a cell membrane.

103693.q: Roughly how thick is a cell membrane?
a: About a tenth of a millimetre
103693.e: A cell membrane is only a few millionths of a millimetre, that is a few nanometres, thick. That is why it can't be resolved on its own with a light microscope.
103693.m: The cell membrane is only a few nanometres thin.

103694.q: Which building blocks in the cell membrane act as channels and pumps for substances?
103694.e: Proteins are built into the fatty double layer of the membrane. Some form channels, others pump substances through the membrane in a targeted way.
103694.m: Proteins in the cell membrane act as channels and pumps.

103695.e: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll. It captures light for photosynthesis.
103695.m: Chlorophyll is the green pigment of chloroplasts.

103696.q: What takes place in the chloroplasts?
103696.e: In the chloroplasts, plants use light to turn water and carbon dioxide into sugar and oxygen. This is photosynthesis.
103696.m: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts.

103697.q: Which energy do chloroplasts use for their work?
103697.e: Chloroplasts convert light energy into chemical energy. That is why green plants need light to grow.
103697.m: Chloroplasts convert light energy into chemical energy.

103698.q: Where are the chloroplasts in a plant cell?
103698.e: The chloroplasts float in the cytoplasm. They are often near the edge of the cell, where they get a lot of light.
103698.m: Chloroplasts are in the cytoplasm of the plant cell.

103699.q: In which cells of a leaf are there especially many chloroplasts?
103699.e: The palisade cells lie directly under the upper surface of the leaf and are packed with chloroplasts. Most photosynthesis takes place there.
103699.m: The palisade cells are the leaf's main power station.

103700.q: Which parts of a plant normally have no chloroplasts?
103700.e: Roots grow in the dark soil and don't carry out photosynthesis. That is why they normally have no chloroplasts.
103700.m: Roots in the soil usually have no chloroplasts.

103702.q: What shape are chloroplasts in land plants usually?
103702.e: In land plants, chloroplasts are usually lens-shaped and only a few thousandths of a millimetre in size. In some algae, however, there are also ribbon-shaped or star-shaped chloroplasts.
103702.m: The chloroplasts of land plants look like little lenses.

103703.q: What happens to the green pigment when a tomato ripens?
a: It is broken down and red pigments form
It gets darker and darker green
103703.e: As it ripens, the tomato breaks down the chlorophyll and forms red pigments. That is why it turns from green to red.
103703.m: Ripe tomatoes break down the green and turn red.

103704.q: What is the job of the large vacuole in a plant cell?
a: It stores water and dissolved substances
It forms the firm cell wall
103704.e: The vacuole is a store full of cell sap. This consists mainly of water with dissolved salts, sugars and pigments.
103704.m: The vacuole is the water store of the plant cell.

103705.q: What is the liquid in the vacuole called?
103705.e: The vacuole is filled with cell sap. This consists mainly of water with dissolved salts, sugars, pigments and other substances.
103705.m: The vacuole is filled with cell sap.

103706.q: What is the pressure called with which the full vacuole presses the cell contents against the cell wall?
103706.e: The internal pressure of a plant cell that is full to bursting is called turgor. It keeps non-woody plant parts such as leaves firm.
103706.m: Turgor keeps leaves and young stems firm.

103707.q: Why does a plant wilt if it gets too little water?
103707.e: Without water the vacuoles shrink and the pressure in the cells drops. The leaves lose their tension and hang down limply.
103707.m: A plant wilts when its vacuoles lose water.

103708.q: What happens to purple red cabbage juice when you add vinegar?
103708.e: The pigments in the cell sap of red cabbage are called anthocyanins. They change colour depending on acidity: with vinegar the juice turns red, with soap rather green.
103708.m: The colour of red cabbage juice shows whether something is acidic.

103709.q: How much of the cell volume can the central vacuole take up in a fully grown plant cell?
103709.e: In fully grown plant cells, the central vacuole often fills most of the cell, up to about 90 per cent of the volume.
103709.m: The central vacuole can fill almost the whole plant cell.

103710.q: How do the vacuoles change as a young plant cell grows?
a: Small vacuoles merge into one large one
The vacuoles move into the nucleus
103710.e: Young plant cells have many small vacuoles. As they grow, they take in water and merge into one large central vacuole.
103710.m: As the cell grows, many small vacuoles become one large one.

103711.q: Which substances do many plants store in the vacuole to protect themselves from animals that eat them?
103711.e: Bitter and poisonous substances are often stored in the vacuole. This puts off animals that feed on the plant.
103711.m: Many plants hide poisons in their vacuoles.

103712.e: The genetic information is in the nucleus in the form of DNA. It contains the blueprints for all the proteins of the cell.
103712.m: The nucleus holds the cell's genetic information.

103713.q: What is the double covering around the nucleus called?
103713.e: The nucleus is surrounded by a nuclear envelope made of two membranes. It separates the genetic material from the rest of the cell contents.
103713.m: The nuclear envelope consists of two membranes.

103714.q: Through which openings do substances get into and out of the nucleus?
103714.e: The nuclear envelope is pierced by many nuclear pores. Substances and messenger molecules pass through them between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
103714.m: Nuclear pores are the gates of the nucleus.

103715.q: Which instrument can you use to see the nucleus of a cell?
103715.e: Cells are far too small for the naked eye. Under the microscope you see the nucleus as a round structure, especially when it is stained.
103715.m: You can only see nuclei under the microscope.

103716.q: What is the dense body in the nucleus where building blocks for ribosomes are made called?
103716.e: In the nucleus you can often see a dark body, the nucleolus. Components of the ribosomes are made there.
103716.m: Building blocks of ribosomes are made in the nucleolus.

103717.q: How many nuclei does an ordinary living plant cell have?
103717.e: A normal plant cell has exactly one nucleus. As the control centre, it directs the processes in the cell.
103717.m: A normal plant cell has a single nucleus.

103718.q: Which cells in human blood have no nucleus?
103718.e: Red blood cells lose their nucleus as they mature. That gives them more room to carry oxygen.
103718.m: Red blood cells have no nucleus.

103719.q: What are the structures called into which the genetic material condenses before a cell divides?
103719.e: Before division, the long DNA is wound up tightly. This forms chromosomes, which can be seen under the microscope.
103719.m: Before division, the genetic material condenses into chromosomes.

a: The cell contents inside the cell membrane, apart from the nucleus
The outer layer of the cell wall
The genetic material in the nucleus
103720.e: The cytoplasm is everything inside the cell membrane except the nucleus. The organelles are found in it.
103720.m: The organelles of the cell are in the cytoplasm.

103721.q: What is cytoplasm mostly made of?
103721.e: Cytoplasm consists mostly of water. Proteins, salts, sugars and many other substances are dissolved in it.

103722.q: What is the movement of the cell contents that you can observe in the small leaves of Canadian waterweed called?
103722.e: In the cells of Canadian waterweed, the cytoplasm constantly flows round in a circle. This cytoplasmic streaming distributes substances in the cell.
103722.m: Cytoplasmic streaming distributes substances in the cell.

103723.q: What is found in the cytoplasm of a cell?
103723.e: The organelles, for example mitochondria and chloroplasts, are found in the cytoplasm. The cell wall lies right on the outside of the plant cell.
103723.m: The organelles are in the cytoplasm.

103724.q: Which organelle in the cytoplasm supplies the cell with energy?
103724.e: In the mitochondria, sugar is broken down with oxygen. This releases the energy that the cell needs.
103724.m: Mitochondria are the power stations of the cell.

103725.q: What gives a plant cell firm support and shape from the outside?
103725.e: The cellulose cell wall surrounds the plant cell like a firm casing. Animal cells have no cell wall.
103725.m: The cell wall gives the plant cell support.

103726.q: Which organelle in the cytoplasm of a plant cell carries out photosynthesis?
103726.e: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll. With it, the plant makes sugar from light, water and carbon dioxide.
103726.m: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts.

103727.q: Where is the cytoplasm in a fully grown plant cell usually found?
a: As a thin layer at the edge
As a ball in the middle
103727.e: The large central vacuole pushes the cytoplasm to the edge. There it forms a thin layer between the vacuole and the cell wall.
103727.m: In old plant cells, the cytoplasm is a thin coating at the edge.

103728.q: What is the job of mitochondria?
a: They release energy through cellular respiration
103728.e: In the mitochondria, nutrients such as glucose are broken down. The cell can use the energy released for its work.

103729.e: Plant cells also need energy for their life processes. That is why they have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts.
103729.m: Plant cells have chloroplasts and mitochondria.

103730.q: Which gas do mitochondria use up during cellular respiration?
103730.e: In cellular respiration, glucose is broken down with oxygen. Without oxygen this process doesn't work.
103730.m: Mitochondria need oxygen for cellular respiration.

103732.q: Why do muscle cells have especially many mitochondria?
a: They need a lot of energy
They store a lot of water
103732.e: Muscles work hard and constantly need energy for it. The mitochondria supply it, which is why muscle cells have especially many of them.
103732.m: Cells that need a lot of energy have many mitochondria.

103733.q: How many membranes surround a mitochondrion?
103733.e: A mitochondrion has a smooth outer membrane and a folded inner membrane. So it is surrounded by two membranes.

103734.q: Which nickname is often used for mitochondria?
103734.e: Because mitochondria provide most of the usable energy, they are often called the power stations of the cell.
103734.m: Mitochondria are called the power stations of the cell.

103735.q: Which substances are produced as waste during cellular respiration in the mitochondria?
103735.e: When sugar is broken down with oxygen, carbon dioxide and water are produced. The carbon dioxide is given off.
103735.m: Cellular respiration produces carbon dioxide and water.

103736.q: An eyepiece magnifies 10 times and the objective lens 40 times. What is the total magnification?
103736.e: You multiply the magnifications of the eyepiece and the objective: 10 × 40 = 400. So the image is magnified 400 times.
103736.m: Total magnification is eyepiece magnification times objective magnification.

103737.q: You move the slide to the left under the microscope. Which way does the image move?
103737.e: A light microscope shows the image upside down and reversed left to right. That is why the image always moves in the opposite direction to the slide.
103737.m: In a microscope the image is upside down and reversed.

103738.q: What is the lens on a microscope that you look into with your eye called?
103738.e: The eyepiece sits at the top of the tube, right at your eye. It is also called the ocular, from the Latin word “oculus” for eye.
103738.m: You look into the microscope through the eyepiece.

103739.q: What is the lens on a microscope that sits just above the specimen called?
103739.e: The objective lens faces the object, that is the specimen. It produces the first magnified image.
103739.m: The objective lens sits just above the specimen.

103740.q: Which part of the microscope do you use to control the amount of light?
103740.e: The diaphragm under the stage lets more or less light through. This is how brightness and contrast are adjusted.
103740.m: You control brightness and contrast with the diaphragm.

103741.q: Which knob do you use first to bring the microscope image roughly into focus?
103741.e: You first use the large coarse focus knob to find a roughly sharp image. Then you adjust it exactly with the fine focus knob.
103741.m: First focus with the coarse knob, then with the fine knob.

103742.q: Which magnification do you start with when using a microscope?
103742.e: With the lowest magnification you see the largest area and find the interesting spot more easily. After that you switch to stronger objectives.
103742.m: When using a microscope, always start with the lowest magnification.

103743.q: Up to what magnification are images from a good light microscope useful?
103743.e: Because of the wavelength of light, images magnified at most about 1,000 to 2,000 times are useful with a light microscope. For more you need an electron microscope.
103743.m: For greater magnification than a light microscope, you need an electron microscope.

103744.q: What is the rotating part that holds several objective lenses called?
103744.e: Objectives with different magnifications are mounted on the objective turret. By turning it you switch quickly between them.
103744.m: You change objectives on the objective turret.

103745.q: Which part of a kitchen onion do you use for an onion skin slide?
a: The thin skin on the inside of a scale
The green shoot in the middle
103745.e: On the inside of a fleshy onion scale there is a wafer-thin skin. It consists of only one layer of cells and is therefore transparent enough for the microscope.
103745.m: For the slide you use the thin inner skin of an onion scale.

103746.q: Why can't you see any chloroplasts in the cells of onion skin?
a: The onion scales grow without light
103746.e: The scales lie inside the onion in the dark and only store nutrients. They don't carry out photosynthesis and therefore have no chloroplasts.
103746.m: Onion skin cells have no chloroplasts because they grow in the dark.

103747.q: What do you put on the slide before laying the onion skin on it?
103747.e: The skin is spread out in a drop of water. That way it doesn't dry out and the cells stay in their natural state.
103747.m: A wet mount lies in a drop of water.

103748.q: How do you put the cover slip on so that no air bubbles form?
a: Lower it at an angle from the side
Let it drop flat onto it
103748.e: You place the cover slip at an angle at the edge of the drop and slowly lower it. This pushes the air out to the side.
103748.m: Lower a cover slip slowly and at an angle.

103749.q: Which stain can be used to colour the nuclei of onion skin cells blue?
103749.e: Methylene blue stains the nuclei in particular a strong blue. That makes them much easier to see under the microscope.
103749.m: Methylene blue makes nuclei easy to see.

103750.q: What do onion skin cells look like under the microscope?
103750.e: Onion skin cells are elongated and lie close together. The image is reminiscent of a brick wall.
103750.m: Onion skin cells lie side by side like bricks.

103751.q: Which tool do you use to peel off the fine onion skin?
103751.e: With the tweezers you grip the thin skin and carefully peel it off. A pipette, on the other hand, is used to drip liquids.
103751.m: The onion skin is peeled off with tweezers.

103752.q: What do you call a slide made from fresh material in a drop of water?
103752.e: A wet mount is made from living material and only lasts a short time. Permanent slides, on the other hand, are preserved and sealed.
103752.m: A wet mount shows living material and doesn't last long.

103753.q: What is the small glass plate you put the specimen on called?
103753.e: The slide is a rectangular glass plate that you put the specimen on. The thinner cover slip goes on top.
103753.m: The specimen lies on the slide.

103754.q: What is the nuclear division called in which two daughter nuclei with the same genetic information are formed?
103754.e: In mitosis, the genetic information is shared out equally between two daughter nuclei. Both daughter cells therefore receive the same genes.
103754.m: Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter nuclei.

103755.q: What must be doubled in the cell before it divides?
103755.e: So that each daughter cell receives the complete genetic information, the DNA is copied exactly beforehand.
103755.m: The genetic material is doubled before every cell division.

103756.q: How many daughter cells are produced in an ordinary cell division?
103756.e: In cell division, one parent cell divides into two daughter cells. Both receive the same genetic information.
103756.m: In division, one cell becomes two.

103757.q: What do living things need cell division for?
a: To grow and to heal wounds
103757.e: Cell division produces new cells. That is how a living thing grows, and how damaged tissue is replaced.
103757.m: Living things grow through cell division.

103758.q: How does a plant cell form the new dividing wall between the daughter cells?
a: Through a cell plate in the middle
By pinching in from the outside
103758.e: In plant cells, a cell plate forms in the middle of the cell and grows outwards. Animal cells, on the other hand, pinch in from the outside.
103758.m: When plant cells divide, they form a new wall in the middle.

103759.q: Where do a plant's cells divide especially often?
a: In the tips of the root and shoot
103759.e: At the tips of roots and shoots there are growth tissues. The cells there divide all the time, and the plant grows longer.
103759.m: Plants grow at their tips through many cell divisions.

103760.q: What is the apparatus of fine fibres that pulls the chromosomes apart during mitosis called?
103760.e: The spindle apparatus consists of fine protein tubes. It attaches to the chromosomes and pulls their halves apart.
103760.m: The spindle apparatus shares the chromosomes out between the daughter cells.

103761.q: What happens to the nuclear envelope at the start of mitosis?
103761.e: At the start of mitosis the nuclear envelope breaks down so that the spindle apparatus can reach the chromosomes. At the end, a new envelope forms around each daughter nucleus.
103761.m: The nuclear envelope breaks down during mitosis and forms again afterwards.

103762.q: Which solution is used in class to test for starch?
103762.e: Iodine solution (iodine in potassium iodide), also called Lugol's solution, reacts with starch and clearly changes its colour. That makes it very easy to detect starch.
103762.m: You test for starch with iodine solution.

103764.q: How can you make starch grains from a potato visible?
a: Cut the potato and look at the juice under the microscope
Freeze the potato and shake it
Dry the potato in the sun
Touch the potato with a magnet
103764.e: If you scrape a little from a cut potato, you can see lots of small starch grains under the microscope. With iodine solution they turn blue-violet.
103764.m: You can see potato starch grains under the microscope.

103765.q: What can you see in potato starch grains under the microscope?
103765.e: Potato starch grains show fine layered rings around a point. They form because the starch is laid down in layers.
103765.m: Starch grains grow in layers like onion rings.

103766.q: Where does a leaf temporarily store starch during the day?
103766.e: When photosynthesis is strong, surplus sugar is stored temporarily as starch in the chloroplasts. At night it is broken down and carried away.
