103766.m: Leaves store starch in the chloroplasts during the day.

103768.q: In which part of a grain of wheat are most of the starch grains found?
103768.e: The endosperm makes up most of the grain and is filled with starch grains. It serves as a food store for the embryo.
103768.m: The endosperm of a cereal grain is full of starch.

103769.q: Plasmodesmata are tiny channels in the cell wall. What do they connect?
103769.e: Plasmodesmata pass through the cell walls of plant cells. In this way the insides of neighbouring cells are connected to each other.
103769.m: Plasmodesmata connect plant cells through the cell wall.

103770.q: What are the fine channels between plant cells, the plasmodesmata, for?
103770.e: Water, sugar and messenger substances pass directly from cell to cell through plasmodesmata.
103770.m: Plasmodesmata allow exchange between plant cells.

103771.q: Why do plant cells need connecting channels like plasmodesmata?
a: Because their firm cell wall would otherwise separate them
103771.e: Plant cells are surrounded by a firm cell wall. Without plasmodesmata they would be cut off from one another.
103771.m: Plasmodesmata pass through the firm cell wall of plant cells.

103772.q: Do animal cells have plasmodesmata too?
a: No, they have no cell wall
103772.e: Plasmodesmata are found in plants, whose cells have a cell wall. Animal cells have no cell wall and are connected in other ways.
103772.m: Plasmodesmata are typical of plant cells.

103773.q: What can pass through the plasmodesmata from one plant cell to the next?
103773.e: The channels are tiny. Only dissolved substances such as water, sugar and messenger substances fit through.
103773.m: Water and sugar pass through plasmodesmata.

103774.q: Some plant viruses use the fine channels between plant cells. What for?
a: To move from cell to cell
103774.e: Many plant viruses widen the plasmodesmata and travel through the plant this way. As they do, the disease spreads.
103774.m: Plant viruses travel from cell to cell through the plasmodesmata.

a: In the cell wall between two plant cells
103775.e: Plasmodesmata cross the cell wall that separates two neighbouring cells. That way the cells stay connected.
103775.m: Plasmodesmata pass through the cell wall.

a: So tiny that you need a very powerful microscope
103776.e: Plasmodesmata are much smaller even than a cell. You can only see them with an electron microscope.
103776.m: You can only see plasmodesmata with a very powerful microscope.

103777.q: Since which year have the Nobel Prizes been awarded?
103777.e: The first Nobel Prizes were awarded in 1901. Since then they have been given almost every year.
103777.m: The Nobel Prizes have existed since 1901.

103778.q: In how many areas were there Nobel Prizes at the start?
103778.e: At the start there were prizes for physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace. That makes five areas.
103778.m: At the start there were five Nobel Prizes.

103779.q: For which school subject is there no Nobel Prize?
103779.e: Alfred Nobel did not plan a prize for maths. Physics, chemistry and literature, on the other hand, are among the Nobel Prizes.
103779.m: There is no Nobel Prize for maths.

103780.q: In which currency is the prize money for a Nobel Prize set?
103780.e: The prize money is set in Swedish kronor, the currency of Sweden. It is several million kronor each time.
103780.m: Nobel Prize money is paid in Swedish kronor.

103781.q: What is the largest number of people who may share a Nobel Prize in one area?
103781.e: A Nobel Prize may be shared between three people at most. That is why some researchers miss out even though they helped.
103781.m: At most three people share a Nobel Prize.

103782.q: In which month do people find out who is getting a Nobel Prize?
103782.e: The winners are announced at the start of October every year. The ceremony only comes later.
103782.m: The Nobel Prizes are announced in October.

103783.q: What did the Geneva scientists Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz receive the Nobel Prize for in 2019?
a: For a planet orbiting another star
103783.e: In 1995 the two discovered the first planet orbiting another star like the Sun. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019.
103783.m: Two Geneva scientists found the first planet orbiting a star like the Sun.

103784.q: Which scientist from Switzerland received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2017?
103784.e: Jacques Dubochet from the canton of Vaud helped to make tiny building blocks of life visible by deep-freezing them. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2017.
103784.m: Jacques Dubochet received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2017.

103785.q: Can you receive a Nobel Prize if you have already died?
a: No, today only living people can
103785.e: Since 1974 Nobel Prizes may no longer be awarded to people who have died. But if someone dies after the announcement, they keep the prize.
103785.m: Today only living people receive Nobel Prizes.

103786.q: Which invention made Alfred Nobel rich?
103786.e: Alfred Nobel invented dynamite, an explosive. It was used, for example, in building tunnels and roads.

103787.q: How did Alfred Nobel make sure that the Nobel Prizes would exist?
103787.e: In his will, Alfred Nobel decided that his fortune should be used for prizes. That is how the Nobel Prizes began.
103787.m: The Nobel Prizes are set out in Alfred Nobel's will.

103788.q: In which year did Alfred Nobel die?
103788.e: Alfred Nobel died in 1896 in Sanremo in Italy. A few years later the first prizes were awarded.

103789.e: Alfred Nobel was a chemist and inventor. He also founded many companies in different countries.
103789.m: Alfred Nobel was a chemist and inventor.

103791.q: Which Nobel Prize is presented in Oslo instead of Stockholm?
103791.e: That is what Alfred Nobel set out in his will. The Nobel Peace Prize is presented in Oslo in Norway, the other prizes in Stockholm.
103791.m: The Nobel Peace Prize is presented in Oslo.

103792.q: In which subject did Albert Einstein receive the Nobel Prize?
103792.e: Albert Einstein was a physicist. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics.
103792.m: Einstein received the Nobel Prize in Physics.

103793.q: Which famous prize did Albert Einstein receive?
103793.e: Einstein received the Nobel Prize in Physics for the year 1921. It was only presented to him a year later.
103793.m: Einstein received the Nobel Prize in Physics.

103794.q: Did Albert Einstein receive the Nobel Prize for the theory of relativity?
a: No, for a discovery about light
103794.e: Einstein received the prize for explaining how light can knock tiny particles out of metal. This is called the photoelectric effect.
103794.m: Einstein received the Nobel Prize for a discovery about light.

103796.q: In which country did Albert Einstein live from 1933 until his death?
103796.e: When the Nazis came to power in Germany in 1933, Einstein left Germany. After that he lived in Princeton in the USA until his death in 1955.
103796.m: Einstein lived in the USA from 1933.

103797.q: Which chemical element was named after Albert Einstein?
103797.e: The artificial element einsteinium bears Einstein's name. In this way the famous physicist is still honoured today.
103797.m: The element einsteinium honours Albert Einstein.

103798.q: In which Swiss city did Einstein work at the patent office when he wrote famous papers in 1905?
103798.e: Einstein worked at the Federal Patent Office in Bern from 1902 to 1909. There, in 1905, he wrote several groundbreaking papers.
103798.m: Einstein wrote his famous 1905 papers in Bern.

103799.q: In which two subjects did Marie Curie receive a Nobel Prize?
103799.e: Marie Curie received one Nobel Prize for physics and one for chemistry. Both had to do with radioactive substances.
103799.m: Marie Curie was honoured in physics and in chemistry.

103800.q: In which year did Marie Curie receive her first Nobel Prize?
103800.e: Marie Curie received her first Nobel Prize in 1903.
103800.m: Marie Curie's first Nobel Prize came in 1903.

103801.q: Who did Marie Curie share her first Nobel Prize with?
103801.e: Three scientists received the first prize together: Marie Curie, her husband Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. All three studied radiation.
103801.m: Marie Curie shared her first prize with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel.

103802.q: In which year did Marie Curie receive her second Nobel Prize?
103802.e: Marie Curie received her second Nobel Prize in 1911.
103802.m: Marie Curie received her second Nobel Prize in 1911.

103803.q: Did Marie Curie receive her second Nobel Prize on her own?
103803.e: Marie Curie received the second Nobel Prize on her own. Her husband Pierre had already died by then.
103803.m: Marie Curie received the second Nobel Prize on her own.

103804.q: In which city was Marie Curie born?
103804.e: Marie Curie was born in Warsaw in Poland in 1867. She later moved to Paris to study.
103804.m: Marie Curie came from Warsaw in Poland.

103805.q: What did Marie Curie become the first person to achieve?
a: A prize at the age of 100
103805.e: Marie Curie was the first person to receive Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. That is a very special achievement.
103805.m: Marie Curie was the first to receive Nobel Prizes in two sciences.

103806.q: In which city is Marie Curie buried?
103806.e: Since 1995 Marie Curie has rested in the Panthéon in Paris. Especially deserving people of France are honoured there.
103806.m: Marie Curie is buried in Paris.

103807.q: What metal is the Nobel Prize medal made of?
103807.e: The Nobel Prize medal is made of gold. It is heavy and very valuable.
103807.m: The Nobel Prize medal is made of gold.

103808.q: Whose face can be seen on the front of the Nobel Prize medal?
103808.e: Alfred Nobel is shown on the front of the Nobel Prize medal. So every medal is a reminder of the man who founded the prizes.
103808.m: Alfred Nobel's face is on the Nobel Prize medal.

103809.q: What shape is a medal usually?
103809.e: A medal is usually a round metal disc, a bit like a large coin.

103810.q: What is a medal often hung around your neck on?
103810.e: Many medals hang on a coloured ribbon. That way you can wear them around your neck.
103810.m: Medals often hang on a ribbon.

103811.q: Which award is often called the “Nobel Prize of mathematics”?
103811.e: The Fields Medal is seen as one of the most important honours in mathematics. It is awarded to young mathematicians.
103811.m: The Fields Medal is the highest honour for mathematicians.

103812.q: How often is the Fields Medal awarded?
103812.e: The Fields Medal is awarded only every four years at a big mathematics congress.
103812.m: The Fields Medal is only awarded every four years.

103813.q: How young do you have to be to receive the Fields Medal?
103813.e: Only mathematicians under 40 receive the Fields Medal. It is meant to honour young talent.
103813.m: Only researchers under 40 receive the Fields Medal.

103814.q: What is often stamped on the back of a winner's medal?
a: The names of all the spectators
103814.e: Medals often say which competition or achievement they were awarded for. Sometimes the year is added too.
103814.m: A medal shows what it was awarded for.

103815.q: On which day are the Nobel Prizes presented in Stockholm?
103815.e: The ceremony takes place on 10 December every year. That is the day Alfred Nobel died.
103815.m: The Nobel Prizes are presented on 10 December.

103816.q: Who presents the Nobel Prizes in Stockholm?
a: The President of the Swiss Confederation
103816.e: In Stockholm the Swedish king hands the prizes to the prizewinners.
103816.m: The Swedish king presents the Nobel Prizes.

103817.q: In which building are the Nobel Prizes presented in Stockholm?
103817.e: The prizegiving takes place in Stockholm's Concert Hall. There is room there for lots of guests and an orchestra.
103817.m: The Nobel Prizes are presented in the Stockholm Concert Hall.

103818.q: What takes place in the evening after the Nobel Prize ceremony?
103818.e: After the ceremony there is a big banquet in Stockholm City Hall. More than a thousand guests eat there together.
103818.m: After the Nobel ceremony there is a big banquet.

103819.q: Which Nobel Prize is presented in Oslo rather than in Stockholm?
103819.e: The Nobel Peace Prize is presented in Oslo in Norway. All the other Nobel Prizes are presented in Stockholm.
103819.m: The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo.

103820.q: What do the prizewinners give in the days before the Nobel Prize ceremony?
a: An exam in front of experts
103820.e: Before the ceremony, the prizewinners explain in a talk what they have discovered. This talk is called the Nobel Lecture.
103820.m: Nobel prizewinners explain their work in a talk.

103821.q: Stockholm is the capital of which country?
103821.e: Stockholm is the capital of Sweden. The city is spread across many islands on the Baltic Sea.
103821.m: Stockholm is the capital of Sweden.

103822.q: What do men usually wear at the Nobel Prize ceremony?
103822.e: The ceremony has a very formal dress code. Men usually wear black tails, women a long evening dress.
103822.m: People dress very formally for the Nobel ceremony.

a: A research competition for young people
103823.e: “Swiss Youth in Science” (Schweizer Jugend forscht) is a foundation. It runs a national competition where young people present their own research.
103823.m: At “Swiss Youth in Science”, young people present their research.

103825.q: What do you need to take part in “Swiss Youth in Science”?
103825.e: Young people submit their own research project, for example their Matura project. A jury decides who gets into the final.
103825.m: At “Swiss Youth in Science” you present your own project.

103826.q: Which piece of school work do upper secondary students often enter for “Swiss Youth in Science”?
103826.e: Many projects are written as a Matura project at upper secondary school (Gymnasium). The best ones can take part in the competition.
103826.m: Many projects at “Swiss Youth in Science” are Matura projects.

103827.q: What is the best rating in the “Swiss Youth in Science” competition?
103827.e: The projects receive ratings such as “good”, “very good” or “excellent”. “Excellent” is the highest level.
103827.m: “Excellent” is the best rating at “Swiss Youth in Science”.

103828.q: What can winners at “Swiss Youth in Science” receive as a special prize?
a: A trip to a competition abroad
103828.e: With special prizes, the best can travel to international competitions or meetings of young scientists, for example in Europe or the USA.
103828.m: The best can present their project abroad.

103829.q: Which “Swiss Youth in Science” activities last a whole week?
103829.e: During the study weeks, young people work together with scientists for a week. That way they get to know real research.
103829.m: In the study weeks, young people do research with experts.

103830.q: What do you present at the “Swiss Youth in Science” final?
103830.e: At the final, the young people stand at a stand and explain their own project to the jury and visitors.
103830.m: At the final, young people explain their own project.

103831.q: What matters most in an inventors' competition?
103831.e: In an inventors' competition, a new and useful idea is what counts most. The jury looks at whether the invention solves a problem.
103831.m: With inventions, a good new idea counts most.

103832.q: What do you call a first test model of an invention?
103832.e: A prototype is the first model of an invention. You use it to test whether the idea really works.
103832.m: A prototype is the first test model of an invention.

103833.q: What can you use to protect an invention from copycats?
103833.e: A patent is a legal protection. For a certain time it forbids others to copy and sell the invention without permission.

103834.q: What is the longest a patent can protect an invention in Switzerland?
103834.e: In Switzerland a patent lasts for 20 years at most. After that anyone may use the invention.
103834.m: A patent protects an invention for 20 years at most.

103835.q: Who decides who wins a competition?
103835.e: A jury is made up of experts. It looks closely at all the entries and chooses the winners.
103835.m: The jury chooses the winners of a competition.

103836.q: In which Swiss city is a big international inventions fair held every year?
103836.e: In Geneva, inventors from many countries show their new ideas every year. The best ones win prizes.
103836.m: Geneva has a big inventions fair.

103837.q: What do you do if your prototype doesn't work on the first try?
a: You improve it and try again
You throw everything away at once
103837.e: Almost no invention works the first time. Inventors look for the mistake, improve their model and test it again.
103837.m: Good inventors don't give up and keep improving their idea.

103838.q: What does an inventor write in their inventor's notebook?
103838.e: In an inventor's notebook you record ideas, drawings and the results of experiments. That way you can look back later at what you tried.
103838.m: An inventor's notebook collects ideas and experiments.

a: A title given as an award without a doctoral thesis
103839.e: You receive an honorary doctorate for special achievements. You don't have to write a doctoral thesis for it.
103839.m: An honorary doctorate is given as an award.

103840.e: Only universities and other institutions of higher education may award the title of honorary doctor.
103840.m: Honorary doctorates are awarded by universities.

103841.q: Which abbreviation comes after the title of an honorary doctor?
103841.e: An honorary doctor writes “Dr. h. c.”. The letters stand for the Latin words “honoris causa”.
103841.m: An honorary doctor has the title “Dr. h. c.”.

103842.q: What does “honoris causa” mean in English?
103842.e: “Honoris causa” is Latin and means “for the sake of honour”. So the title is an honour and not a university degree.

103843.q: Do people who never went to university sometimes get an honorary doctorate?
103843.e: People without a degree can also get an honorary doctorate, for example for art, music or helping other people.
103843.m: You can get an honorary doctorate without a degree.

103844.q: What do professors at some universities wear at a formal honorary doctorate ceremony?
103844.e: At some universities, professors and the people being honoured wear long robes called gowns at ceremonies.
103844.m: At formal ceremonies, some professors wear a gown.

103846.q: What do you think up before an experiment?
103846.e: Before the experiment you think about what will probably happen. You then test this prediction with the experiment.
103846.m: Before an experiment you make a prediction.

103847.q: Why do scientists repeat an experiment?
a: So that they can be sure
103847.e: If an experiment gives the same result several times, the result is more reliable. A single experiment could turn out a certain way by chance.
103847.m: Repeating experiments makes a result more reliable.

103848.q: How do children often present their results at science competitions?
103848.e: On a poster you can show the question, the experiment and the result clearly with pictures. That way visitors understand the project quickly.
103848.m: A poster presents a science project clearly.

103849.q: What is the name of the Swiss foundation where young people can present their research projects?
103849.e: At “Schweizer Jugend forscht” (Swiss Youth in Science), young people present their own research projects. Germany has a similar competition called “Jugend forscht”.
103849.m: In Switzerland the research competition is called “Schweizer Jugend forscht”.

103850.q: Who decides which project wins a prize at a science competition?
103850.e: A jury is a group of experts. It looks closely at all the projects and decides who gets a prize.
103850.m: A jury decides on the prizes.

103851.q: What do you write down carefully during an experiment?
a: What the weather will be tomorrow
103851.e: Scientists note down exactly what they see, measure and observe. These notes are called a record or report.
103851.m: During an experiment you write down your observations.

103852.q: What is especially important in experiments for children?
103852.e: You have to be careful in experiments, for example with fire or hot water. That is why you ask adults for help.
103852.m: When doing science, safety always comes first.

103853.e: A trophy cup is a fine vessel that you receive for a win. It often looks like a big cup.
103853.m: A trophy cup is a winner's cup.

103854.q: What was a trophy cup originally used for?
103854.e: A cup like this used to be a large drinking vessel. The German word for it, “Pokal”, comes from the Italian word for jug.
103854.m: People used to drink from cups like these.

a: A trophy that is passed on every year
103855.e: You only keep a challenge trophy until the next competition. Then it goes to the new winner.
103855.m: A challenge trophy moves from winner to winner.

103856.q: What is often engraved on a trophy?
a: The winner's name and the year
The names of all the spectators
103856.e: Many trophies show who won and in which year. That way the trophy reminds people of the victory.
103856.m: A trophy often shows the winner's name.

103857.q: How many handles does a classic trophy cup often have?
103857.e: Many classic trophy cups have one handle on each side, so two. That makes them easy to lift up.
103857.m: Many trophy cups have two handles.

103858.q: Where do schools or clubs often display their trophies?
103858.e: In a display cabinet with glass doors, trophies are easy to see and protected. That way everyone can admire the successes.
103858.m: Trophies are often shown in a display cabinet.

103859.q: What is the difference between a trophy and a medal?
a: You stand a trophy up, you wear a medal
You wear a trophy, you stand a medal up
Trophies are only for second place
103859.e: You hang a medal around your neck. A trophy, on the other hand, you put on a table or a shelf.
103859.m: You wear a medal and stand a trophy up.

103860.e: A certificate is an important document. It confirms, for example, a victory or a special achievement.
103860.m: A certificate confirms something in writing.

103861.q: What makes a certificate genuine and valid?
103861.e: A responsible person signs a certificate. That shows who issued it.
103861.m: A signature makes a certificate valid.

103862.q: What is written on a winner's certificate?
103862.e: A winner's certificate shows who achieved what and when. That way it can be proven later.
103862.m: A winner's certificate names the person, the achievement and the date.

103863.q: At which event do schoolchildren often get a certificate?
103863.e: On sports day, children show how fast they can run and how far they can throw. There is often a certificate for it.
103863.m: There is often a certificate on sports day.

103864.q: Where do many people keep an important certificate?
a: In a frame on the wall
103864.e: Many people frame their certificates and hang them up. That way they stay nice and everyone can see them.
103864.m: Important certificates are often framed and hung up.

103865.q: Which certificate is issued when a child is born?
103865.e: After a birth, a birth certificate is issued. It confirms the name, date of birth and place of birth.
103865.m: Every child gets a birth certificate when they are born.

103866.q: What is often pressed onto an official certificate in addition to the signature?
103866.e: Official certificates often carry the office's stamp as well as the signature. It shows that the certificate is genuine.
103866.m: A stamp shows that a certificate is genuine.

103867.q: Can a person have several honorary doctorates?
103867.e: Different universities can honour the same person. Some famous people therefore have dozens of honorary doctorates.
103867.m: Famous people often have several honorary doctorates.

103868.q: What does it mean to defend a trophy?
103868.e: If you defend a trophy, you win the competition again the next time. That way the trophy stays with the same winner.
103868.m: You defend a trophy by winning again.

103869.q: Which document do you often get after passing a course?
103869.e: A diploma is a certificate. It confirms that you have successfully completed a course or training.
103869.m: A diploma confirms a successful qualification.

103870.q: In which city was Albert Einstein living when he received the Nobel Prize?
103870.e: From 1914 to 1932, Einstein lived and did research in Berlin. He was living there when he won his Nobel Prize.
103870.m: At the time of his Nobel Prize, Einstein lived in Berlin.

a: Something new that didn't exist before
Something you find in the forest
103871.e: An invention is a new thing or a new method. It did not exist in that form before.
103871.m: An invention is something completely new.

103872.q: Who is the national competition of “Schweizer Jugend forscht” mainly for?
a: Young people at upper secondary and vocational schools
103872.e: The participants are mainly young people from grammar schools, specialised secondary schools and vocational schools.
103872.m: The competition is mainly for young people from upper secondary and vocational schools.

103873.q: Who chooses the winners of the Nobel Prize in Physics?
103873.e: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences chooses the winners for physics and chemistry. It considers nominations from experts all over the world.
103873.m: A Swedish academy chooses the Nobel Prize winners in physics.

103874.q: Which two large joints does the humerus form part of?
103874.e: At the top, the head of the humerus sits in the socket of the shoulder blade; at the bottom the bone forms the elbow joint with the ulna and radius.
103874.m: The humerus connects the shoulder with the elbow.

103875.q: Which two bones join the humerus at the elbow?
103875.e: There are two bones in the forearm, the ulna and the radius. Together with the humerus they form the elbow joint.
103875.m: The humerus, ulna and radius meet at the elbow.

103876.q: What kind of joint does the head of the humerus form with the shoulder blade?
103876.e: The round head of the humerus sits in a socket of the shoulder blade. That is why you can move your arm in almost every direction.
103876.m: The shoulder joint is a ball and socket joint.

103877.q: What is the round upper end of the humerus called?
103877.e: The upper end of the humerus is a half ball covered with cartilage. It glides in the joint surface of the shoulder blade.
103877.m: The head of the humerus is the round end of the bone.

103878.q: Which large shoulder muscle is attached to the side of the humerus and lifts the arm sideways?
103878.e: The deltoid covers the shoulder like a cap and is attached to a rough spot on the shaft of the humerus. It lifts the arm sideways.
103878.m: The deltoid forms the round shoulder and lifts the arm.

103879.q: Which part of the humerus breaks especially often in older people after a fall?
a: The upper end near the shoulder
The lower end at the elbow
The groove of the radial nerve
103879.e: A fracture near the head of the humerus is one of the most common fractures in older people. The bone is often weakened by bone loss.
103879.m: In old age the upper arm often breaks near the shoulder.

103880.q: Which part of the skeleton does the humerus belong to?
103880.e: Arms and hands together form the upper limb. The humerus is its top and longest bone.
103880.m: The humerus is the longest bone of the arm.

103881.q: What else can be injured when the humerus breaks?
a: A nerve that controls the hand
103881.e: An important nerve, the radial nerve, runs around the shaft of the humerus. If it is injured in the fracture, the hand can hang limp.
103881.m: When the upper arm breaks, a nerve can be injured.

103882.q: On which side of the forearm is the ulna?
a: In the middle of the back of the hand
103882.e: If you hold your palm facing forwards, the ulna lies on the inside, on the little finger side.
103882.m: The ulna is on the little finger side.

103883.q: Which part of the ulna forms the hard point of the elbow?
103883.e: The upper end of the ulna forms a strong projection, the olecranon. You feel it when you lean on your elbow.
103883.m: The point of the elbow belongs to the ulna.

103884.q: Which forearm bone is the stronger one near the elbow?
103884.e: The ulna is thick at the top near the elbow and carries the large olecranon there. Towards the wrist it gets narrower.
103884.m: At the elbow, the ulna is the thick bone.

103885.q: Which of the two forearm bones is longer in adults?
a: It differs from arm to arm
103885.e: The ulna reaches from the elbow to the wrist and sticks out above the radius at the top with the olecranon. That is why it is a little longer.
103885.m: The ulna is the longer forearm bone.

103886.q: What is the Latin technical term for this forearm bone on the little finger side?
103886.e: In technical language the bone is called the ulna. The name of the ulnar nerve, nervus ulnaris, comes from it, for example.
103886.m: The forearm bone on the little finger side is called the ulna.

103887.q: How many long bones make up the forearm?
103887.e: The forearm has two long bones: the ulna on the little finger side and the radius on the thumb side.
103887.m: The forearm is made up of the ulna and the radius.

103888.q: Which forearm bone is the humerus’s most important partner at the elbow?
103888.e: The ulna grips the pulley-shaped end of the humerus with a pincer-like notch. This is where the arm bends and straightens.
103888.m: At the elbow, the ulna forms a hinge with the upper arm.
